6.s:
The Union of India includes which of the following?

A. States

B. Union Territories

6.x: The 'Union of India' includes only the States, which share powers with the Union; UTs and acquired territories are part of the 'Territory of India', not of the Union. So A only.

6.s: First schedule of constitution contains the
o: List of States and Union Territories
Allocation of Seats for States in Lok Sabha
Allocation of functions and powers between Union and States
6.x: The First Schedule lists the States and Union Territories and their territories. Seats in the Lok Sabha are not in the First Schedule, and languages are in the Eighth.

6.s:
The 'Territory of the 'Union of India' are two distinct and different expressions due to which of the following reason/reasons?
I. The 'Union of India' includes just States and Union Territories while the 'Territory of India' includes in addition to States and Union Territories, those territories that may be acquired by the Government of India at any future time as well.
II. The expression 'Union of India' is mentioned in the Constitution of India, but the expression 'Territory of India' is not found in the Constitution of India.
III. The First Schedule of the Constitution of India| is with reference to just the 'Union of India' but not the 'Territory of India'.
IV. The Union Territories are covered by the expression 'Territory of India' and not by the expression 'Union of India'.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below: IV.
6.x: The 'Union of India' includes only the States; the 'Territory of India' covers States, UTs and territories that may be acquired, so IV is correct. I is wrong (the Union does not include UTs), II is wrong (both expressions are in Art. 1) and III is wrong (the First Schedule lists States and UTs). Only IV.

6.s: The territories of different states and union territories under the Union of India is specified in which of the following Schedules?

6.s: If a new State of the Indian Union is to be created, which one of the following Schedules of the Constitution must be amended?

6.x: In N. Masthan Sahib v. Chief Commissioner, Pondicherry the SC held that 'acquired' in Art. 1(3)(c) means acquisition as understood in public international law (cession, conquest, occupation). Acquired territory falls within Art. 1 and need not join an existing State (it can be a UT).

C is incorrect (India is quasi-federal) and D is incorrect as FRs can be amended but not removed (basic structure). So B, C and D.

8.s: How can Parliament amend a Fundamental Right?
o: Only by a constitutional amendment, subject to the basic structure
8.x: Fundamental Rights can be altered only by the amendment procedure, subject to the basic-structure doctrine of Kesavananda Bharati (1973); an ordinary law cannot amend the Constitution.
xa: Other limits on FRs: **Arts. 31A-31C**.
The **Ninth Schedule** protection is limited by **I.R. Coelho (2007)**.

8.s: Who can impose reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights.
8.x: Reasonable restrictions are imposed by law made by Parliament (legislature); courts only judge their reasonableness.

8.s: The Parliament has enacted Army and Air Force Acts of 1950 to restrict the application of Fundamental Rights of Defence Personnel. This Power of Parliament lies under this Article of the Constitution.
8.x: Art. 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the FRs of armed forces etc.; the Army Act and Air Force Act 1950 were made under it. Art. 34 is martial law, 35 legislation on Part III.

8.s: A proclamation of National Emergency automatically suspends
8.x: Under Art. 358, a National Emergency (war/external aggression) automatically suspends Art. 19, the Right to Freedom; other FRs need a Presidential order under Art. 359, and Arts. 20-21 are never suspended.

8.s: One among the following is authorized to impose restrictions of Fundamental Rights:
8.x: Reasonable restrictions on FRs are imposed by law made by the legislature – Parliament – not by the President or Prime Minister (the President only suspends enforcement during an emergency). (Printed key President corrected.)

8.x: Art. 33 lets Parliament restrict the FRs of the armed forces; Arts. 19, 21 and 25 are rights, not restricting powers.

8.s: The President of India has the power to suspend the
8.x: Under Art. 359 the President can suspend the enforcement of Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency (except Arts. 20 and 21, so not Art. 21 or 21A specifically).

o: Members of the forces charged with the responsibility of maintenance of public order
Members of the forces employed in connection with the communications systems set-up in the country
Members of the forces employed in connection with the communication systems set-up for maintenance of public order
8.x: Art. 33 covers the armed forces, forces for public order and persons in communication systems set up for those forces; staff of communication systems in the country in general are not covered and enjoy FRs like other citizens. So option C is the odd category in the list (answer C, as in the published key). (Printed key A corrected.)

8.s: Under Article 33, who has the power to restrict the Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces?
8.x: Article 33 gives the power exclusively to Parliament, and it may extend to non-combatant employees such as cooks and barbers.
xa: **Art. 34**: restrictions while **martial law** is in force; Parliament may pass an **indemnity** Act.
FRs can be limited only by a **constitutional amendment**, subject to the **basic structure**.

8.x: Since the 44th Amendment (1978), enforcement of Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Art. 359. Arts. 14, 19, 22 and the right to move courts under Art. 32 for other rights can be affected by such an order, so the other pairs are wrong.
xs: **Articles 20 and 21** can never be suspended — option **(2)**.
This is the **44th Amendment, 1978** limit on **Art. 359**.
xa: Under Art. 359 the **President** suspends **enforcement** of named FRs by order.
The **44th Amendment 1978** also removed the **Right to property (Art. 31)**.
⚠ "All FRs are suspended in an emergency" is **false** (APPSC GS **2019**).

8.x: Article 34 concerns restrictions during martial law and indemnity by Parliament; Article 33 deals with the armed forces.

8.x: Article 35 gives this power to Parliament alone, for uniformity.

8.x: Art. 13(2): the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges FRs; such a law is void to that extent.

8.s: X was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term 'law' as provided under Article 13, Part III of the Constitution of India. X explained that the meaning of the term 'law' in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. Y pointed out that the term 'law' in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which 'X' was not convinced. Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below:
o: X is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom.
The view of Y that 'law' included custom is not correct.
The views of both 'X' and 'Y' are correct.
The view of only Y is correct.
8.x: Art. 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification and custom or usage having the force of law. X's denial that custom is included contradicts the text, so only Y's view is correct.

8.s: Which Article of the Constitution gives precedence to Constitutional provisions over the laws made by the Union Parliament/State Legislatures?
8.x: Article 13 voids laws of Parliament and State legislatures inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights, giving constitutional (Part III) provisions precedence; Art. 245 is the extent of laws, 32 remedies, 326 adult suffrage.

o: Kesavanand Bharti Vs. State of Kerala

8.x: Golaknath (1967) held that Parliament cannot amend (abridge) Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda (1973) later allowed amendment subject to the basic structure.

8.s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court

8.x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
8.tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
xs: Under **Art. 13(3)**, "law" includes **ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage** — option **(1)**.
Amendments under **Art. 368** are excluded by **Art. 13(4)** (**24th Amendment 1971**) — option (2) wrong.
xa: **13(1):** pre-constitution laws inconsistent with FRs are **void** to that extent.
**13(2):** the State shall not make a law **abridging FRs**.
**Art. 13** makes FRs **supreme over ordinary law**.

o: Treated as ordinary laws under Article 13

Twin test for classification: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus**.

xs: The twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus with the object** — option **(3)**.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.
xa: Reiterated **Apr 2026**: the State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** (Kerala/KSRTC).

**Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: any **arbitrary action** violates Art. 14.

**E.P. Royappa (1974)**: equality is **antithetic to arbitrariness**.

18.x: Article 368 (Part XX) lays down Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and its procedure; the other Articles (emergencies 352/356/360, 366-367 definitions, 369-370 temporary provisions) are not about amendment.

18.s:
The Indian Constitution is often described as a unique blend of rigidity and flexibility. Which of the following provisions reflect this dual nature?

1. Certain constitutional amendments require a special majority in Parliament.

2. Some provisions can be amended by a simple majority, like ordinary laws.

3. Fundamental Rights can be amended without judicial review.

4. The federal structure of the Constitution cannot be altered easily.
18.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
18.x: Special majority (1), simple majority for some provisions (2) and the hard-to-alter federal structure (4) show the blend. Statement 3 is wrong: FR amendments are subject to judicial review (basic structure).

18.s:
The Constitution of India is often described as neither rigid nor flexible, but a blend of both. Which of the following reasons justify this statement?

1. The Indian Constitution can be amended as per the choice of the Lok Sabha.

2. Some constitutional amendments require approval from state governments.

3. Before introducing any constitutional amendment bill, the President's permission is required to check Parliament's functioning.

4. Different types of parliamentary resolutions require different types of majorities for passage.
18.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
18.x: Some amendments need State ratification (2) and different matters need different majorities (4). The Lok Sabha alone cannot amend (1), and no prior Presidential permission is needed (3).

18.s: The constitutional amendment procedure in India was borrowed from which country?
18.x: India borrowed the amendment procedure from South Africa. The method of electing members of the Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.
18.tq: Test the source of a constitutional feature while avoiding confusion with countries associated with other federal provisions.
xs: The amendment procedure was borrowed from **South Africa** — option **(2)**.
South Africa also gave the **election of Rajya Sabha members**.
⚠ Not the **US**, whose Constitution is **very rigid**.
xa: India's procedure is partly rigid, partly flexible — unlike the flexible **British** one.
**Granville Austin**: "one of the **most ably conceived aspects**" of the Constitution.
Location: **Part XX, Article 368**.

18.s: Which of the following expressions is used in Article 368 to describe Parliament’s constituent power to amend the Constitution?
o: May, in exercise of its judicial power, interpret or repeal any provision
Shall, in exercise of its constituent power, amend every provision by referendum
May, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision
May, in exercise of its legislative power, repeal only those provisions approved by the States
18.x: Article 368 states that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
18.tq: Select the precise constitutional wording and reject substitutions of legislative or judicial power.
xs: Art. 368: Parliament "**may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal** any provision" — option **(3)**.
The power lies with **Parliament** alone — no referendum and no prior State approval, so (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Limit: Parliament **cannot alter the basic structure** (**Kesavananda Bharati, 1973**).
The amending power includes **Fundamental Rights**, by special majority.
Art. 368 is the **sole Article** of **Part XX**.

18.s: Who described the constitutional amendment process as appearing 'complicated' but being 'merely diverse'?
18.x: Granville Austin said the process appears complicated but is merely diverse, calling it one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution.
xa: The procedure is a **synthesis** of rigidity and flexibility.
Three routes: **simple majority**, **special majority**, **special majority + State ratification**.

18.s: As of 2026, which is the latest constitutional amendment to have been enacted in India?
18.x: The 106th Amendment (2023) is the latest enacted amendment. The 101st (2016, GST) and 104th (2020) are earlier enactments, and the 131st was only a Bill that failed in the Lok Sabha in April 2026.
18.tq: Latest enacted = 106th (2023); 129th and 131st are Bills only.
xs: The latest enacted amendment is the **106th Amendment (2023)** — option **(3)**.
The **101st (2016)** is older — it added the **GST Council (Art. 279A)** to the federal list.
The **131st (2026)** was only a **Bill**, negatived in the Lok Sabha on **17 April 2026**.
xa: The **129th Bill, 2024** (simultaneous elections, **Art. 82A**) is with a **Joint Committee**.
The **24th (1971)** made the President's **assent** to amendment bills obligatory.

18.s: Which Article and Part of the Constitution govern the amendment powers and procedure?
18.x: Article 368, in Part XX, gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and sets the procedure. Article 356 is President's Rule and 280 the Finance Commission.
18.tq: Recall Article 368 and Part XX.
n: Article 368 in Part XX governs the amendment power and procedure of the Indian Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xs: Amendment powers and procedure are in **Article 368 in Part XX** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 368** is the **sole Article** of **Part XX**; Parliament amends "**by way of addition, variation or repeal**".
**Articles 280, 324, 356** are not amendment provisions.
xa: The procedure was borrowed from **South Africa**.
The Constitution is **neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis of both**.
**Granville Austin**: the process "appears complicated" but "**is merely diverse**".

18.s: Which one of the following best characterises the nature of the Indian constitutional amendment procedure?
o: It is entirely flexible because every provision can be changed by ordinary law.
It is rigid only in matters relating to Fundamental Rights.
It is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility.
It is entirely rigid because every provision requires State ratification.
18.x: The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
18.tq: Compare the constitutional system as a whole instead of applying one amendment method to every provision.
xs: The procedure is a **synthesis of rigidity and flexibility** — option **(3)**.
It is **neither purely rigid nor purely flexible**: some provisions change by **simple majority**, others by **special majority**, some also need **State ratification**.
Only **federal provisions** need ratification by **half the States** — so (4) is wrong.
xa: Unlike the **very rigid US** Constitution and the **flexible British** one.
**Granville Austin**: the process "**appears complicated**" but "**is merely diverse**".
Source of the procedure: **South Africa**.

18.s: Besides the 24th Amendment, which Amendment amended Article 368 itself?
18.x: Article 368 was amended by the 24th (1971) and the 101st (2016) Amendments.
18.tq: one-liner

18.s: Who described the Indian Constitution as 'quasi-federal' and praised its balance between rigidity and flexibility?
18.x: K.C. Wheare called the Constitution quasi-federal and saw a good balance of rigidity and flexibility in its amendment procedure.

18.s: By which Amendment was Article 13(4) inserted?
18.x: The 24th Amendment inserted Article 13(4), clarified Parliament's power to amend FRs and made presidential assent to amendment Bills obligatory.
xa: The **25th (1971)** replaced "compensation" with "**amount**" and inserted **Art. 31C**.
Both came in **1971**; the **42nd (1976)** followed as the "**Mini-Constitution**".

18.x: Under Art. 368(2) an amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament, not in State legislatures.

Consider the following statements.

I. The Amendment procedure has been provided in Article-368 of the Constitution of India.

II. The consent of the states is mandatory for all Amendments to the Constitution of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
18.x: I is true (Art. 368). II is false: only amendments to federal provisions need ratification by half the States.

18.s:
Consider the following statements :

A. A bill amending the Constitution requires a prior recommendation of the President of India.

B. When a Constitution Amendment Bill is presented to the President of India, it is obligatory for the President of India to give his/her assent.

C. A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a special majority and there is no provision for joint sitting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: A is false: no prior recommendation of the President is needed. B is true (24th Amendment: 'shall give his assent'), and C is true: special majority in each House, no joint sitting.

18.s:
With reference to the procedure for Amendment of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
I. A private member of the House of the Parliament can introduce the Bill for amendment of the Constitution only after the prior permission of the President.
II. Article 368 of the Constitution of India provides for three types of amendments-simple majority, special majority and ratification of half of the States by a simple majority.
III. For amendments that require ratification of half 55. the States by a simple majority, it is not necessary that all the State Legislatures must take action on the Bill.
IV. The State Legislatures can pass a resolution requesting the Parliament to amend Article 368 in the same manner, as it could be done for the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in the States. Which of the statement / statements given above is / are correct?
18.x: Only III is right: half the States suffice, so not every State must act. I is false (no prior permission), II is false (Art. 368 provides two types; simple majority is outside it), and IV is false (the resolution route exists only for Councils, Art. 169).

18.s: Which one of the following Bills must be passed by each House of the Indian Parliament separately, by special majority?
18.x: A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by each House separately by a special majority; there is no joint sitting. Ordinary, Money and Finance Bills need a simple majority.

18.s: Which one of the following Bills must be passed by each House of the Indian Parliament separately by the special majority?
18.x: Only a Constitution Amendment Bill must pass each House separately by special majority (total membership plus two-thirds present and voting).

18.s: Consider the following statements regarding Constitutional Amendments: (i) In Article 368, two methods of Constitutional Amendment are mentioned. (ii) Constitutional Amendment Bill can be initiated only in Lok Sabha. (iii) In case of any dispute between two Houses of Parliament on Constitutional Amendment Bill, Joint sitting of both Houses can be summoned. (iv) The President can not veto a Constitutional Amendment Bill. Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: (i) is true: Art. 368(2) has two methods. (iv) is true: the President must assent. (ii) is false because either House may initiate, and (iii) is false because there is no joint sitting.

18.s:
Consider the following statements: An amendment of the Constitution of India can be initiated by the
I. Lok Sabha
II. Rajya Sabha
III. State Legislatures Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 33
IV. President
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
18.x: An amendment can be initiated only by a Bill in the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. State Legislatures only ratify, and the President does not initiate.

18.s:
An amendment to the Constitution of India can be initiated by the:
1. Lok Sabha
2. Rajya Sabha
3. State Legislatures
4. President
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
18.x: Only the two Houses of Parliament can initiate an amendment Bill; State Legislatures and the President cannot.

18.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. An amendment to the Constitution of India can be initiated by an introduction of a Bill in Lok Sabha only.

II. If such an amendment seeks to make changes in the federal character of the Constitution, the amendment also requires to be ratified by the legislature of all the States of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
18.x: Both false: a Bill may be introduced in either House, and federal amendments need ratification by half the States, not all.

18.s: What does the Constitution provide in case of a deadlock between the two Houses over an Ordinary Bill?
o: Passage by the Lok Sabha alone
A final decision by the President
18.x: An ordinary Bill needs a simple majority, both Houses have equal powers over it, and a deadlock can go to a joint sitting.
n: The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha have equal legislative powers over an Ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
An Ordinary Bill is passed by a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting is possible for an Ordinary Bill in case of a deadlock. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider an Ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: A **Money Bill** originates in the **Lok Sabha only**; Rajya Sabha gives only **recommendations** within **14 days**.
A **Money Bill** has **no joint sitting**.
An **Amendment Bill** needs a **special** majority and has **no joint sitting**.

18.s: In which manner may a Bill for amendment of the Constitution be introduced?
o: By a minister or a private member, without the President's prior permission
Only by a minister, with the President's prior permission
Only after ratification by the States
18.x: An amendment Bill needs no prior presidential permission and may be moved by a private member; Article 108 joint sittings do not apply to it.
xa: Exam angle: "prior permission", "joint sitting" and "President may return" are all **false** for amendment bills.
The President's assent is **obligatory** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).

18.s: By which Amendment was it made obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill?
18.x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 made the President's assent to a constitutional amendment bill obligatory.
18.tq: Match the precise amendment with the specific procedural change rather than the more famous 42nd or 44th Amendments.
xs: The **24th Amendment Act, 1971** made the President's **assent** to amendment bills obligatory — option **(1)**.
The 24th answered **Golaknath (1967)** and restored Parliament's power to amend FRs.
xa: It amended **Arts. 13 and 368** and inserted **Art. 13(4)**: an Art. 368 amendment is not "law" under Art. 13.
The **42nd (1976)** later inserted **368(4) and (5)**, struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

18.s: Which type of Bill may require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures?
o: Constitution Amendment Bill affecting federal provisions
18.x: Constitution Amendment Bills affecting specified federal provisions need ratification by at least half the States; ordinary Bills need only a simple majority in Parliament.

18.s: Where must a Constitution Amendment Bill be passed by a special majority?
o: A joint sitting of both Houses
The Lok Sabha, with recommendations from the Rajya Sabha
18.x: An amendment Bill can start in either House without the President's recommendation and needs a special majority in each House separately; there is no joint sitting.
n: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed separately by each House by a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill cannot be passed through a Joint Sitting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill does not require the President’s prior recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting under Article 108 is not applicable to a Constitution Amendment Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: Special majority = majority of **total membership** + **two-thirds** present and voting.
A **private member** may move it; a **State Legislature** cannot introduce one.
The President **must** give assent — made mandatory by the **24th Amendment (1971)**.

18.s: What does a special majority for amending the Constitution mean?
o: Three-fourths of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting
A majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
18.x: Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
18.tq: Do not substitute two-thirds of total membership or a joint sitting for the two-part constitutional formula.
xs: Special majority = a **majority of the total membership** of each House + **two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(3)**.
It applies in **each House separately**; there is **no joint sitting** — so (4) is wrong.
**Two-thirds of total membership** (2) is the **Art. 61** type — impeachment of the President.
xa: Art. 368 type also used for removal of **SC/HC judges** (**124, 217**), **CAG (148)**, **CEC (324)**, **SEC (243K)**, approval of **National Emergency (352)**.
**Art. 249/312** type: two-thirds present and voting in the **Rajya Sabha only**.

18.s: By what majority does a State Legislature ratify a Constitution Amendment Bill?
o: Two-thirds of members present and voting
Majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting
18.x: Ratification is by a simple majority of each concerned State Legislature, and no time limit is prescribed for it.

18.s: What can the President do once a Constitution Amendment Bill is duly passed?
o: May withhold assent in the public interest
May return it once for reconsideration
May refer it to a joint sitting
18.x: Assent to a duly passed amendment Bill is obligatory: the President can neither withhold it nor return the Bill (24th Amendment, 1971).

18.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about presidential action on Bills?
o: The President may return a Money Bill once for reconsideration
The President may return an Ordinary Bill once
The President may withhold assent to an Ordinary Bill
The President may withhold assent to a Money Bill
18.x: A Money Bill can be assented to or withheld but never returned; only an ordinary Bill can be returned once.
n: The President may assent to, withhold assent from, or return an Ordinary Bill once. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President may assent to or withhold assent from a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President cannot return a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: **Amendment Bill**: the President **must give assent** — **no veto**, no power to return.
Mandatory assent was added by the **24th Amendment (1971)**.
A Money Bill needs the President's **prior recommendation**; an Amendment Bill does **not**.

18.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the passage of Bills?
o: A Money Bill originates only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha may only make recommendations
An Ordinary Bill may originate in either House, with equal powers for the Rajya Sabha
A Financial Bill (I) can only be recommended on, not rejected or amended, by the Rajya Sabha
A Constitution Amendment Bill may originate in either House and must pass each House separately
18.x: A Financial Bill (I) originates only in the Lok Sabha, but the Rajya Sabha has full power to reject or amend it.
n: A Financial Bill (I) may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has full power to reject a Financial Bill (I). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has full power to amend a Financial Bill (I). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for an Ordinary Bill may be the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for a Money Bill is the Lok Sabha only. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for a Constitution Amendment Bill may be the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has equal powers over an Ordinary Bill and may amend or reject it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill, and its consideration is limited to 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has equal powers over a Constitution Amendment Bill, which must be passed separately by both Houses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
An Ordinary Bill may originate in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: Money Bills: **Arts. 109 and 110**; Ordinary: **107 and 108**; Amendment: **368**.
Rajya Sabha has **14 days** for a Money Bill; **no fixed time limit** for an Ordinary Bill.
**Joint sitting** (**Art. 108**) only for Ordinary Bills.

18.s: What happens if either House of Parliament rejects a Constitution Amendment Bill?
o: A joint sitting is summoned to resolve it
18.x: There is no joint sitting for a Constitutional Amendment Bill, so rejection by either House causes failure; once duly passed, assent is obligatory under the 24th Amendment.
xa: Criticism: there is no mechanism to resolve a **deadlock** between Houses on an amendment.
The President can neither **withhold** nor **return** the bill.

18.s: Which Article on joint sittings does NOT apply to Constitution Amendment Bills?
18.x: Article 108 (joint sitting) does not apply to amendment Bills, so each House must pass them separately.
18.tq: one-liner

18.s: How is a deadlock between the two Houses on a Constitution Amendment Bill resolved?
o: By a joint sitting under Article 108
There is no mechanism: a joint sitting is not available
By ratification of half the States
By reference to the Supreme Court
18.x: The Constitution provides no joint sitting for amendment Bills, so a deadlock cannot be resolved; this absence is itself a criticism of the procedure.

18.s: Regarding the amendment of the Constitution all following statements are correct, except
o: According to Article 368, Parliament of India can amend any part of the Constitution
Article 2 of the Constitution empowered the Parliament of India to admit new states into the Union
With reference to Article 2 or 3, the amendment of the provisions of FIRST and FOURTH schedule shall not be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purpose of Article 368
The territories of the units of the federation may be altered or re distributed by the Parliament without intimation to the States
18.x: The wrong statement is the last one: under Art. 3 the Bill needs the President's recommendation and is referred to the affected State legislature for its views, so States are intimated. The others are correct (Art. 368 wording, Art. 2, Art. 4(2)).

18.s: What type of majority is needed to amend provisions related to acquisition and termination of citizenship?
18.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
18.x: Acquisition and termination of citizenship is regulated by Parliament by simple majority, outside Art. 368.

18.s: Article 32 of the Constitution
o: Can be amended with simple majority
Can be amended with two-thirds majority
Can be amended with ratification by the States
18.x: Article 32, like all Fundamental Rights, is amended by a special majority (two-thirds present and voting plus a majority of total membership), without State ratification.

18.s: The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India can be amended by:
18.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
18.x: The Fifth and Sixth Schedules can be amended by Parliament by a simple majority (para 21 of the Sixth Schedule); this is not an Art. 368 amendment.

o: a special majority with ratification of the concerned states
a simple majority with ratification of the concerned states

18.x: A law creating a new State under Arts. 2-3 is passed by a simple majority and is not deemed an amendment (Art. 4(2)), so no special majority or ratification is needed.

18.s: The formation of new states and the alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing states can be done through:
o: special majority of the Parliament and the ratification of at least half of the state legislatures
18.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
18.x: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names is by simple majority of Parliament (Arts. 3-4).

18.s: Which of the following is the procedure to abolish or create Legislative Council in a State
o: On the recommendation of State Legislature bypassing a resolution with 2/3 majority, followed by an act of parliament
18.x: Under Art. 169 the State Assembly passes a resolution by special majority (two-thirds present and voting plus majority of total membership), followed by an Act of Parliament. It is not an Art. 368 amendment.

18.s: Creation of a new state requires a ....... majority for Constitutional Amendment.
o: Two-third plus ratification by half of all states
18.x: Creation of a new State needs only a simple majority; Art. 4 says such a law is not an amendment for Art. 368.

18.s: A Bill for the purpose of creating a new State in India must be passed by
o: A simple majority in Parliament and ratification by
A two-third majority in Parliament and ratification by
18.x: A Bill creating a new State is passed by a simple majority in Parliament; no special majority or State ratification is needed.

18.s: The Provisions which CANNOT be amended by simple majority and which do NOT require Ratification by States are amended by:
18.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
18.x: Provisions outside the simple-majority list and not needing ratification are amended by a special majority of Parliament; ordinances, Cabinet decisions or Presidential orders cannot amend the Constitution.

18.s: By which procedure can Article 32 be amended?
o: A special majority plus ratification by half the States
A special majority of Parliament without State ratification
No procedure, as it cannot be amended at all
18.x: Article 32 may be amended by special majority without State ratification, though the Supreme Court's power under it is part of the basic structure.
xa: **PYQ G2 2017** key: Art. 32 needs a "**two-thirds majority**".
All **FRs** (incl. Art. 32) and **DPSPs** fall in the special-majority route.

18.s: Which of the following is required to amend the Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Special majority plus ratification by half the States
18.x: DPSPs, like Fundamental Rights, are amended by special majority without State ratification.

18.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 2 to Article 4 — Formation and alteration of States
Article 169 — Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils
18.x: Article 368 contains the general constitutional amendment procedure, whereas citizenship is among the matters that can be changed by simple majority under Article 11. Articles 2–4, 169 and 327 relate to the subjects stated.
18.tq: Use the wrong Article-subject pairing trap and verify the provision against the subject.
xs: **Article 368 — Citizenship** is wrong — option **(4)**.
Citizenship is **Art. 11**, changed by **simple majority**; **Art. 368** is the amendment procedure.
**Art. 327** (elections, delimitation), **Arts. 2-4** (States) and **Art. 169** (Legislative Councils) are correct.
xa: **Art. 343**: **official language** — also simple majority.
Simple-majority changes are **not counted as Art. 368 amendments**.

18.s: Which one of the following subjects is amended by a simple majority of Parliament outside the procedure of Article 368?
18.x: Quorum is among the matters that can be altered by a simple majority outside Article 368. Fundamental Rights and DPSPs require the special majority procedure, while the election of the President also requires State ratification.
18.tq: Use the amendment-method classification to identify the simple-majority exception.
xs: **Quorum in Parliament** is changed by **simple majority**, outside Art. 368 — option **(4)**.
**FRs** and **DPSPs** need a **special majority** under Art. 368.
**Election of the President** also needs **State ratification**.
xa: Other simple-majority items: **salaries of MPs**, **privileges**, **citizenship (11)**, **official language (343)**, **Fifth and Sixth Schedules**.
Such changes are **not deemed amendments** under Art. 368.

18.s: Which of the following is required to create or abolish a State Legislative Council under Article 169?
o: A simple majority of Parliament, outside Article 368
A special majority plus ratification by half of the States
A special majority of the State Legislature only
18.x: Legislative Councils are dealt with by simple majority outside Article 368; the President's election needs special majority plus State ratification.
xa: States can only pass a **resolution** asking Parliament to create/abolish a Council.

18.s: How can changes relating to Articles 2, 3 and 169 of the Constitution be made?
o: A special majority plus ratification by half the States
A simple majority, without being deemed amendments under Article 368
18.x: Changes under Articles 2, 3 and 169 are made by simple majority and are not deemed amendments under Article 368; the Constitution has both flexible and rigid methods.
xa: Other simple-majority items: **citizenship (11)**, **official language (343)**, **delimitation (327)**.
⚠ Exam: "Which is NOT amended by special majority?" — official language, citizenship, **Fifth/Sixth Schedule**.

18.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 2 deals with the admission or establishment of new States.
Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are amendments under Article 368.
Article 3 deals with the formation of new States and alteration of boundaries.
18.x: B is incorrect: Article 4 says laws under Articles 2 and 3 are NOT amendments under Article 368 — they pass by simple majority. The others are right: Article 2 new States, Article 3 boundaries, Articles 5–11 citizenship.
18.tq: Watch for a dropped 'not'.
n: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 3 concerns the formation of new States and alteration of State boundaries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not constitutional amendments under Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Articles 5 to 11 concern citizenship. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Article 4** makes laws under **Articles 2 and 3** amendments under **Article 368** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 4(2)**: such laws are **not amendments under Art. 368**; they pass by **simple majority**.
**Art. 2** = **admission or establishment** of new States; **Art. 3** = **formation of new States** and boundaries; **Arts. 5 to 11** = **citizenship**.
xa: **Article 11**: Parliament's power to **regulate** citizenship.
**Art. 169** (Legislative Councils) is also changed by simple majority, outside Art. 368.

o: Free and compulsory education for children upto the
Organization and working of co-operative societies
Stringent measures to deal with terrorism
Provision of Lokpal to prevent corruption
20.x: The 97th Amendment (2011, notified 12 Jan 2012) gave constitutional status to co-operative societies: Art. 19(1)(c), Art. 43B and Part IXB. It has nothing to do with education, terrorism or Lokpal.

20.s: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2012 is concerned with ......
o: free and compulsory education for children upto the age of 14 years.
organisation and working of co-operative societies.
stringent measures to deal with terrorism.
provision of Lokpal to prevent corruption.
20.x: The 97th Amendment (2011, notified 12 Jan 2012) gave constitutional status to co-operative societies: Art. 19(1)(c), Art. 43B and Part IXB. It has nothing to do with education, terrorism or Lokpal.

20.s:
Which of the following statements are true regarding 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011?
A. Gave Constitutional status and protection to Co-operative Societies.
B. Made the right to form Co-operative Societies a Fundamental Right under Article 19.
C. It added a new Part IX-B to the Constitution.
D. Added new Directive Principle under Article 43-B.
20.x: All four are true: constitutional status for co-operatives, the right under Art. 19(1)(c), Part IXB and DPSP Art. 43B.

20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: 97th Amendment (2011) – Part IX-B, permitting a maximum of 31 directors under Article 243ZJ
91st Amendment (2003) – Barred defectors from ministerial posts (Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A))
101st Amendment (2016) – GST and the GST Council under Article 279A
20.x: Article 243ZJ, added by the 97th Amendment, permits a maximum of 21 directors, not 31.
n: The 91st Amendment was enacted in 2003. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 91st Amendment inserted Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 91st Amendment barred defectors from ministerial posts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment was enacted in 2011. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment added Directive Principle Article 43B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment added Part IX-B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX-B contains Articles 243ZH to 243ZT. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Article 243ZJ provides for a maximum of 21 directors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 100th Amendment was enacted in 2015. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 100th Amendment operationalized the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement involved the exchange of 111 Indian enclaves and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment was enacted in 2016. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Goods and Services Tax became effective on 1 July 2017. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment created the GST Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The GST Council is provided under Article 279A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX-B was added by the 97th Amendment in 2011. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **91st** enforced the **15%** ceiling on the **Council of Ministers**.
GST became effective on **1 July 2017**.

20.s: Under Article 243ZJ, what is the maximum number of directors on a co-operative board?
20.x: The 97th Amendment's Article 243ZJ caps the board at 21 directors, not 31.

20.s: What is the term of the board of a co-operative society under the constitutional provisions?
20.x: The board has a five-year term; the provisions also fix a maximum of 21 directors, one SC/ST seat, two women seats and audit within six months.
xa: Elections must be held **before the term expires**.
**Rajendra N. Shah (2021)**: Part IXB survives only for **multi-State** co-operatives.

20.s: In which case did the Supreme Court strike down Part IXB insofar as it applied to State co-operative societies?
o: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)
20.x: In Rajendra N. Shah (2021), Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT, added by the 97th Amendment) was struck down for State co-operatives as State ratification was absent.
xa: India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives (**2026**).

20.s: Which Article was inserted into the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 97th Constitutional Amendment?
20.x: Article 43B was inserted to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
20.tq: Use the exact Article number rather than confusing it with the adjacent Article 43A.
xs: The **97th** inserted **Article 43B** into the DPSPs — option **(2)**.
43B: **voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control, professional management** of co-operatives.
xa: The 97th also made forming **co-operative societies** a Fundamental Right under **Art. 19(1)(c)**.
New **Part IXB** (**Arts. 243ZH-243ZT**).
Board: **maximum 21** directors; **5-year** term.

20.s: In Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021), why was Part IXB held inapplicable to State co-operative societies?
o: It dealt exclusively with municipal bodies
It had been repealed by the 105th Amendment
It had not been ratified by the States as required
20.x: The Supreme Court struck down Part IXB in its application to State co-operative societies because the required ratification by the States had not been obtained. It continues to operate for multi-State co-operative societies.
20.tq: Connect the judicial outcome with the precise constitutional procedural defect.
xs: Part IXB fell for **State** co-operatives as it had **not been ratified by the States** as required — option **(4)** (**Rajendra N. Shah, 2021**).
It **survives** for **multi-State** co-operatives.
xa: Part IXB came by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.
The 97th also amended **Art. 19(1)(c)** and added **Art. 43B**.
India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives.

20.s: Under the 97th Amendment, for whom must a co-operative board reserve seats?
o: Two SC/ST members and one woman
One SC/ST member and two women
20.x: Co-operative boards reserve one seat for SC/ST and two for women, with a 5-year term.

20.s: Which Article was amended by the 97th Amendment to make the right to form co-operative societies a Fundamental Right?
20.x: The 97th Amendment (2011) added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c); Article 43B is the Directive Principle it added.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about Part IXB (co-operative societies):
1. A co-operative board can have a maximum of 21 directors.
2. The accounts must be audited within six months of the close of the financial year.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Both are correct: Article 243ZJ caps the board at 21 directors, and audit must be done within six months of the end of the financial year.

20.s: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was created by which Amendment?
20.x: The 99th Amendment (2014) created the NJAC, which the Supreme Court struck down in 2015 for violating judicial independence.
n: The 99th Amendment was enacted in 2014. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 99th Amendment created the National Judicial Appointments Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission as unconstitutional in 2015. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission for violating judicial independence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The NJAC case (**SC Advocates-on-Record Assn.**) was decided **4:1**.
**Independent judiciary** is part of the **basic structure**.
The **100th (2015)** = **India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement**.

20.s: In which year did the Supreme Court strike down the 99th Amendment, which created the National Judicial Appointments Commission?
20.x: The 99th Amendment (2014) creating the NJAC was struck down in 2015 to protect judicial independence.

20.s: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was provided for by which Amendment?
20.x: The 99th Amendment, 2014 provided for the NJAC, struck down in 2015; the 97th, 100th and 102nd dealt with co-operatives, the Land Boundary Agreement and the NCBC.

20.s: Which of the following is the latest enacted Constitutional Amendment Act?
20.x: The 106th Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 2023, is the latest enacted amendment in the sequence. The 105th Amendment of 2021 is therefore not the latest.
20.tq: Avoid the stale-current-affairs trap by identifying the highest enacted amendment number and year.
xs: The **106th Amendment, 2023** is the **latest enacted** amendment — option **(4)**.
⚠ UPSC notes calling the **105th** "the most recent" are **stale**.
xa: The 106th gives **one-third seats for women**.
⚠ **103rd and 104th** are both **2019** — EWS and SC/ST seats to **2030**.
Pending: **129th** (ONOE), **130th** (detained ministers); the **131st** was **defeated**.

20.s: The 100th Amendment implemented the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement covering how many Indian enclaves?
20.x: The 100th Amendment (2015) covered 111 Indian and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves.

20.s: Which recent Constitutional Amendment is the only one struck down as a whole by the Supreme Court?
20.x: The 99th Amendment (NJAC) was struck down as a whole; the 97th was struck down only in part (Rajendra N. Shah).

20.s: Which Article inserted by the 101st Amendment created the GST Council?
20.x: Article 279A created the GST Council; 246A gives concurrent GST power and 269A covers inter-State supply.

20.s: Which Article was omitted by the 101st Amendment?
20.x: The 101st omitted Article 268A (service tax) and inserted 246A, 269A and 279A.

20.s: What does Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, provide for?
o: Power of both Parliament and States to make GST laws
20.x: 246A lets Parliament and the States both make GST laws; 269A is inter-State supply and 279A the GST Council.

20.s: By what majority does the GST Council take its decisions?
20.x: The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, decides by a three-fourths majority.

20.s: From which date was the Goods and Services Tax, introduced by the 101st Amendment, rolled out?
20.x: The 101st Amendment got assent on 8 September 2016 and GST came into effect from 1 July 2017.

20.s: Who chairs the GST Council under Article 279A?
o: The Chairman of the Finance Commission
20.x: The GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and decides by a three-fourths majority.

20.s: The Constitution Bill (103rd Amendment), 2017 deals with
o: empowers National Commission on Backward Classes
empowers National Council for Backward Classes
empowers National Council for Scheduled Castes
empowers National Commission for Scheduled Castes
20.x: The 2017 Bill (Constitution 123rd Amendment Bill, enacted as the 102nd Amendment, 2018) gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (Art. 338B). It is a 'Commission', not a 'Council'.

20.s: Which Article, inserted by the 102nd Amendment, gave constitutional status to the NCBC?
20.x: Article 338B made the NCBC constitutional; 342A lets the President notify the SEBC list.

20.s: Through which Article did the 105th Amendment restore the States' power to identify their own SEBCs?
20.x: The 105th inserted 342A(3), letting States/UTs identify their own SEBCs.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the 102nd and 105th Amendments:
1. The 102nd Amendment received assent on 11 August 2018.
2. The 105th Amendment took away the States' power to identify SEBCs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the 105th restored the States' power to identify SEBCs.

20.s: Which Constitutional Amendment gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes?
20.x: The 102nd Amendment, 2018 inserted Article 338B and made the NCBC a constitutional body.

20.s: With which of the following is the 104th Amendment associated?
20.x: The 104th ended Anglo-Indian nominations; EWS came with the 103rd, GST with the 101st and women's reservation with the 106th.
n: The One Hundred and First Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 114-117]
The One Hundred and Third Constitutional Amendment Act provided 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 114-117]
The One Hundred and Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act ended Anglo-Indian nominations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 114-117]
The ending of Anglo-Indian nominations became effective in January 2020. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 114-117]

20.s: The 103rd Amendment was passed as which Constitution Amendment Bill?
20.x: The EWS amendment was passed as the 124th Amendment Bill, 2019.

20.s: By what majority did the Supreme Court uphold the 103rd Amendment in Janhit Abhiyan (2022)?
20.x: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (7 Nov 2022) upheld the EWS amendment by 3:2.

20.s: Which Constitutional Amendment extended the reservation of seats under Article 334 up to 2030 and also ended the nomination of Anglo-Indians to legislatures?
20.x: The 104th Constitutional Amendment, 2019, extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs up to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.
20.tq: Use the paired consequence—extension plus ending Anglo-Indian nomination—to identify the amendment.
xs: The **104th Amendment (2019)** extended **SC/ST seats to 2030** and **ended Anglo-Indian nomination** — option **(1)**.
The **101st** was **GST** — option (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ The **103rd** (also **2019**) gave **10% EWS** reservation.
The **106th (2023)**: **one-third seats for women**.

20.s: Which clauses did the 103rd Amendment insert for EWS reservation?
20.x: The 103rd inserted 15(6) for education and 16(6) for jobs, up to 10% for EWS.

20.s: On which date did the 103rd Amendment receive Presidential assent?
20.x: The 103rd received assent on 12 January 2019; 7 November 2022 is the Janhit Abhiyan judgment.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022):
1. It upheld the 103rd Amendment by a 3:2 majority.
2. It held that the 50% ceiling applies to EWS reservation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the 50% ceiling applies to 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4), not EWS.

20.s: Under the 103rd Amendment, up to what household income limit is a family treated as Economically Weaker Section (EWS) for reservation?
20.x: The 10% EWS quota under Articles 15(6) and 16(6) covers households with income up to Rs 8 lakh.

20.s: From which month and year did the nomination of Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies end?
20.x: The 104th Amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination, effective January 2020.

20.s: Up to which year did the 104th Amendment extend SC/ST seat reservation under Article 334?
20.x: The 104th extended SC/ST seat reservation in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies to 2030.

20.x: The 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) received assent on 28 September 2023.

20.s: Which Article inserted by the 106th Amendment reserves seats for women in State Legislative Assemblies?
20.x: Article 332A covers State Assemblies; 330A covers the Lok Sabha and 334A the timing.

20.s: For how many years does women's reservation under the 106th Amendment last, unless extended by Parliament?
20.x: It lasts 15 years from commencement, extendable by Parliament by law.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the 106th Amendment (women's reservation):
1. The reservation starts only after delimitation based on the first Census taken after its commencement.
2. The reservation lasts 15 years and cannot be extended by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: The quota begins only after delimitation on the first Census after commencement. It lasts 15 years but Parliament can extend it by law, so statement 2 is wrong.

20.s: To the completion of which of the following has the implementation of women's reservation under the 2023 law been linked?
20.x: The women's reservation remains unimplemented because its implementation is linked to the completion of delimitation.
xa: A **revised delimitation bill** is expected.
The **131st Bill, 2026** on delimitation was **defeated** (**17 Apr 2026**).
Southern States fear a **smaller share** after delimitation.

20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 106th Constitutional Amendment?
o: It has been criticised for not providing a separate sub-quota for BC women
Southern States fear their share may decline after delimitation
It has already been implemented in all State Legislative Assemblies
It provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
20.x: The women's quota under the 106th Amendment remains unimplemented.
xa: The LoP asked why the **2023** law was tied to **delimitation** (Aug **2026**).
Local bodies: one-third for women since **1992** (**Arts. 243D, 243T**).

20.s: Under which Articles has one-third reservation for women in Panchayats and Municipalities been provided since 1992?
20.x: Articles 243D and 243T deal with reservation in Panchayats and Municipalities respectively, giving women one-third seats since 1992.
xa: The **106th (2023)** extends **one-third seats for women** to legislatures — still **unimplemented**.
Criticism: **no BC sub-quota** in the 106th.

20.s: In which year did the 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) receive Presidential assent?
20.x: It received assent on 28 September 2023.

20.s: Under which Article are seats reserved for women in the Lok Sabha by the 106th Amendment?
20.x: Article 330A covers the Lok Sabha; 332A State Assemblies; 243T is municipal women's reservation.

20.s:
Consider the following statements concerning the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016:

A. The Act introduced Goods and Service Tax (GST).

B. The Act amended Sixth and Seventh Schedules of Indian Constitution.

C. The Act empowered Karnataka Governor to take steps for developing Hyderabad-Karnataka region.

D. The Act provided for the composition and function of National Judicial Appointments Commission.
Choose the correct answer from the following:
o: Both A and B are correct
A, B, C and D are correct
20.x: The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and amended the Sixth and Seventh Schedules. Statement C is the 98th Amendment (2012, Art. 371J) and D the 99th (2014, NJAC).

20.s: Which of the following Articles is proposed to be inserted by the 129th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2024?
20.x: The 129th Amendment Bill proposes insertion of Article 82A and amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327 in connection with simultaneous elections.
20.tq: Identify the newly proposed Article while separating it from Articles inserted by enacted amendments.
xs: The **129th Bill, 2024** proposes **Article 82A** (One Nation, One Election) — option **(2)**.
It also amends Arts. **83, 172, 327**.
xa: It came with a **UT Laws Bill**; introduced **17 Dec 2024**.
JPC chair: **P.P. Chaudhary**.

20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2025?
o: It concerns removal of the PM, CMs and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges
It increases the Lok Sabha strength to 850 members
20.x: Raising the Lok Sabha to 850 was the 131st Bill; the 130th concerns removal of Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days and amends Articles 75, 164 and 239AA.

20.s: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024 on One Nation, One Election inserts Article 82A. Which Articles does it amend?
20.x: The 129th Bill amends Articles 83, 172 and 327; 75, 164 and 239AA belong to the 130th Bill.

20.s: Who chairs the Joint Parliamentary Committee examining the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 on One Nation, One Election?
20.x: The 129th Amendment Bill on simultaneous elections is with a JPC chaired by P.P. Chaudhary.

21.s: In which case, Supreme Court of India propounded the doctrine of basic structure of Indian Constitution?
21.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer Screening Test General Studies
21.x: The basic structure doctrine was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Indra Sawhney is on reservation, Maneka Gandhi on Art. 21 and Minerva Mills (1980) only applied the doctrine.

21.s: In which of the following cases, the Supreme Court of India enunciated the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’?
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973, 13 judges, 7:6) enunciated the doctrine: Parliament may amend but not 'damage or destroy the basic structure'. Golaknath, A.K. Gopalan and Maneka Gandhi did not.

21.s: In which of the following cases the Supreme Court regarded Preamble as a part of the basic structure of India Constitution?
21.x: In Kesavananda Bharati the Court held the Preamble is part of the Constitution and its objectives form part of the basic structure. Berubari (1960) had held the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.

21.s: The Supreme Court of India enunciated the doctrine of ‘Basic Structure of the Constitution’ in
21.x: The doctrine was first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), not in Golaknath (1967), Sajjan Singh (1965) or Shankari Prasad (1951), which dealt with the amendability of FRs.

21.s: In which case(s) did the Supreme Court of India give for the first time the doctrine of 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
o: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills vs. Union of India
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) first laid down the basic structure doctrine and overruled Golaknath. Golaknath had denied the power to amend FRs; Minerva Mills only applied the doctrine, so 'both' is wrong.

21.s: The Keshavananda Bharati Case is important because-
o: It sets aside the orders of the executive
The Supreme Court interpreted the basic features of
It brought the Union Government in the dock
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati is important because the Supreme Court interpreted the basic features (basic structure) of the Constitution there. It was not about setting aside executive orders.

21.s: The doctrine of 'basic structure' in the context of Indian Constitution was propounded in which of the following cases for the first time?
o: Sankari Prasad V. Union of India
Champakam Dorairajan V. State of Madras
Kesavananda Bharati V. State of Kerala
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) first propounded the basic structure doctrine. Shankari Prasad and Golaknath dealt with amending FRs, and Champakam Dorairajan with communal reservation.

21.s: Which one of the following cases outlined the basic structure doctrine of the Indian Constitution?
21.x: The doctrine was outlined in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), which overruled Golaknath; Gopalan dealt with preventive detention.

21.s: The concept of ‘Basic Structure of the Constitution’ was propounded by the Supreme Court in the case of
o: Keshvanand Bharti vs State of Kerala – 1973
21.x: The doctrine was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Golaknath (1967) only limited Parliament's power to amend FRs; Yusuf and Chitralekha are unrelated.

21.s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution was propounded by the Supreme Court of India in the case of
o: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala
Shankari Prasad vs. Union of India
21.x: The basic structure theory was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), not Golaknath or Shankari Prasad.

21.s: The Supreme Court of India has propounded the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’ of the Constitution in which of the following cases?
21.x: The doctrine owes its origin to the majority judgment in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), later approved in Minerva Mills (1980).

21.s: The ‘Basic Structure Doctrine’ was enunciated by the Supreme Court during the
21.x: The doctrine was enunciated in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which overruled Golaknath; Maneka Gandhi and Bommai came later and did not originate it.

21.s: For which one of the following judgements of Supreme Court of India, the Kesavananda Bharti vs State of India case is considered a landmark?
o: The religion cannot be mobilised for political ends.
Right to Life and Liberty cannot be suspended under any circumstance.
The basic structure of the Constitution, as defined in the Preamble, cannot be changed.
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati is the landmark for the basic structure doctrine: the objectives in the Preamble embody the basic structure, which cannot be changed under Art. 368. The other options are unrelated.

21.s: Which one of the following cases propounded the concept of ‘Basic structure’ of the Indian Constitution?
21.x: The doctrine was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which is not among options A–C: Indra Sawhney is on reservation, Shankari Prasad upheld amending FRs, Rudul Shah is on compensation. So 'None of the above'.

21.s: Who argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law?
21.x: German jurist Dietrich Conrad argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
21.tq: Pair the jurist with both the year and the country from which the idea was drawn.
xs: **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India in **1965** that the amending power has **implied limits** — option **(3)**.
His argument drew on **Germany**'s **Basic Law** and is treated as the **origin of the idea** of basic structure.
xa: **Justice Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**".
CJI **S.M. Sikri** headed the **13-judge bench** in Kesavananda Bharati.
The doctrine was **first propounded** in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

21.s: The idea of implied limits on the amending power was drawn from the Basic Law of which country?
21.x: Dietrich Conrad drew on Germany's Basic Law in arguing for implied limitations in 1965.
21.tq: one-liner

21.s: Who headed the 13-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati?
21.x: CJI S.M. Sikri headed the 13-judge bench; Mudholkar dissented in Sajjan Singh and Conrad was a German jurist.
21.tq: one-liner

21.s: The dissent of Justice Mudholkar in which case first referred to the idea of ‘basic features’ of the Constitution?
21.x: Justice Mudholkar’s dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to the idea of basic features.
21.tq: Test the precursor observation rather than the later case that formally propounded the doctrine.
xs: Justice **Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**" — option **(3)**.
**Sajjan Singh** upheld the **17th Amendment** and reaffirmed **Shankari Prasad**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** came later and **first propounded** the doctrine itself.
xa: Jurist **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India (**1965**) that the amending power has **implied limits**.
**Golaknath (1967)** overruled both Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
First application of the doctrine: **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.

21.s: Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973) was decided by a 13-judge bench by what majority?
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority.

21.s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
xs: Kesavananda struck down the part **barring courts from questioning** whether a law gives effect to the **Directive Principles** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **judicial review is basic**.
The **Ninth Schedule** came from the **1st Amendment** with **Art. 31B**, not Art. 31C; the power to amend FRs was **upheld** (24th Amendment).
xa: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** for **Art. 39(b), (c)** laws.
The **42nd** widened it; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck the widened form down.
Art. 31C = DPSP primacy — a **Parliament**-made rule, not a judge-made doctrine.

21.s: What is the present position on the Preamble?

Part of the Constitution but not amendable at all
The sole content of the basic structure

21.x: The basic structure theory is a product of judicial interpretation (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); it is not written in the Constitution, a statute or the opinion of jurists.

21.s: The Objectives specified in the Preamble contain the basic structure of our Constitution. In this regard, choose the correct answer.
o: Basic structure means that which can be amended with a simple majority
Basic structure means that which cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Article 368 of the Constitution
Basic structure refers to the Directive Principles only
Basic structure refers to Fundamental Rights only
21.x: Basic structure means the features that cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368 (Kesavananda, 1973). It is not limited to the DPSPs or the FRs, and nothing in it is amendable by simple majority.

21.s: The basic structure theory of the Constitution of India implies that –
o: Certain features of the Constitution are so essential to
Fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away
The Constitution cannot be amended except in
The Preamble of the Constitution cannot be amended
21.x: The theory means certain features of the Constitution are so essential that they cannot be abrogated even by amendment. FRs can still be abridged, and the Preamble can be amended, subject to the basic structure.

21.s: The doctrine of 'the Basic structure of the Constitution' as a principle of Judicial Review
o: Accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts
Accepts the theory of supremacy of Legislature
Assumes the power of judging the Legislature
Is strictly in accord with the Principle of Procedure established by Law
21.x: By reviewing even constitutional amendments, the doctrine accepts the supremacy of the Constitution and of the courts (judicial supremacy 'to a limited extent'). It is not 'strictly in accord with procedure established by law' – under that principle a court only checks that the authority acted within its powers, so option D is wrong.

21.s:
Consider the following statements about the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution:

III. Parliament's limited power to amend the Constitution is also an element of the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

o: The order in which the Articles of the Constitution are arranged cannot be altered
Constitutional amendments by Parliament can be only on procedural matters

Constitution is foundation of the basic rights

Origin of the idea: jurist **Dietrich Conrad** (1965) argued that the amending power has **implied limits**.

o: Provided the basic structure is not damaged
Only outside the scope of Article 368

21.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Golaknath case (1967)?

21.s: In which case was the basic structure doctrine applied for the first time, with free and fair elections treated as a basic feature?

xs: The doctrine was first applied in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** — option **(2)**.
The **39th Amendment** clause putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts (**Art. 329A(4)**) was struck down; **free and fair elections** held basic.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** concerned the **42nd Amendment**; **Waman Rao (1981)** the cut-off date; **Golaknath (1967)** predates the doctrine.
xa: The case also held **democracy, rule of law, judicial review** basic.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also tied **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
In **2026**, free and fair elections as basic structure were cited in the debate on making **voting** a fundamental right.

21.s: Which of the following provisions introduced or widened by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills?
o: Articles 368(4) and 368(5), and the widened Article 31C
21.x: Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5), which sought to make Parliament's amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable, along with the widened form of Article 31C.
21.tq: Use the specific amendment-provision pairing rather than identifying the case by name alone.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)** and the **widened Art. 31C** — option **(2)**.
These **42nd Amendment (1976)** clauses excluded **judicial review** and claimed unlimited amending power.
**Art. 329A(4)** fell in **Raj Narain (1975)**; the **NJAC** fell in **2015**; the Ninth Schedule was never struck down as a whole.
xa: Minerva Mills held **judicial review**, **limited amending power** and **FR-DPSP harmony** basic.
**Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** and widened by the **42nd**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws.

21.s: By what majority did the Supreme Court strike down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act in 2015?

xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Golaknath 6:5**, **Kesavananda 7:6**, **NJAC 4:1**.
**Independent judiciary** was earlier held basic in **All India Judges Association (2002)**.
**Judicial review** is basic — **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

o: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Indira Sawhney v. Union of India

II. The validity of law placed in 9th schedule cannot be examined by any court and no judgement can be made on it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Consider the following statements:

A. The Parliament of India can place a particular law in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India.

B. The validity of a law placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be examined by any court and no judgement can be made on it.
Which of the Statements given above is/are correct?
21.x: A is correct: Parliament places laws in the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendment. B is wrong: after I.R. Coelho (2007) such laws can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.

21.s: In which year was the Waman Rao judgment on the Ninth Schedule delivered?
21.x: Waman Rao came in 1981, after the First Amendment (1951) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and before I.R. Coelho (2007).
xa: Waman Rao's cut-off date (**24 April 1973**) is the date of Kesavananda.
In between: **Golaknath (1967)**, **24th Amendment (1971)**, **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
Later: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**; **NJAC case (2015)**.

21.s: What is the position of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973?
o: Open to review on the basis of the basic structure
21.x: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973 as the cut-off; post-cut-off entries are open to basic-structure review rather than enjoying immunity.
xa: **24 April 1973** is the date of the **Kesavananda Bharati** judgment.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**, a **nine-judge bench**, rejected **blanket immunity**.
Waman Rao applied the cut-off to **Ninth Schedule/Art. 31A** laws.

21.s: Which of the following was NOT associated with the First Amendment Act, 1951?
o: Addition of public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement as grounds under Article 19(2)
