xa: **2026 = 75 years** of the 1st Amendment (18 June 2026); assent by President **Rajendra Prasad**.
The Ninth Schedule began with **13** Acts; now **282**.
**I.R. Coelho** limit was restated on the 1st Amendment's **75th** year.

21.s: Which one of the following statements about the Ninth Schedule is correct?
o: It contains only laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c).
It contains fewer than 50 entries and enjoys complete immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not confer blanket immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, and its contents have no constitutional relationship with Fundamental Rights.
21.x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
21.tq: Reject the absolute claim of complete immunity and combine the numerical fact with the judicial limitation.
xs: The Ninth Schedule has grown to **more than 280** entries, but inclusion **does not confer blanket immunity** — option **(3)**.
It started with **13** Acts and now has **282**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: **no blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**; it covers land-reform laws, not only Art. 39(b), (c) laws.
xa: Its purpose: protect **land-reform/zamindari-abolition** laws from challenge for violating **Fundamental Rights**.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** are open to basic-structure challenge.
Laws enter it **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.

21.s: By which of the following can a law be placed in the Ninth Schedule?
o: A State Legislature by ordinary law
21.x: Inclusion needs a constitutional amendment by Parliament; the Schedule covers Central and State laws and was created mainly for land-reform laws.
xa: Created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
Size: **13** Acts at start → **282** now.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: post-1973 entries can be tested on basic structure.

21.s: Tamil Nadu's law providing 69 per cent reservation was placed in the Ninth Schedule by which Constitutional Amendment?
21.x: The Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994.
21.tq: Link the famous law with its specific amendment number and year.
xs: The **76th Amendment Act, 1994** placed Tamil Nadu's **69%** reservation Act in the Ninth Schedule — option **(1)**.
It shows that laws enter the Ninth Schedule **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.
xa: Since such an entry came after **24 April 1973**, it is open to basic-structure review (**Waman Rao**, **I.R. Coelho**).
**I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)**: post-1973 laws invalid if they abrogate the essence of **Arts. 14, 19, 21**.
The Schedule covers **both Central and State laws**.

21.s: The I.R. Coelho case applied the ‘rights test’ or ‘direct impact test’ primarily with reference to the essence of which Articles?
21.x: Under the rights or direct-impact test, a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of the rights protected under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
21.tq: Separate the three Articles in the direct-impact test from other Fundamental Rights provisions.
xs: The **rights / direct-impact test** looks at the essence of **Arts. 14, 19 and 21** — option **(1)**.
Under **I.R. Coelho (2007)**, post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are invalid if they damage the basic structure or abrogate the essence of these Articles.
xa: Coelho was decided by a **nine-judge bench**.
**Arts. 31A, 31C** save certain laws from **Arts. 14, 19**.
**No blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**.

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 31B — Laws concerning acquisition of estates and agrarian reform
Article 31A — Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C — Laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c)
Article 350A — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
21.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
21.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.
xs: **Art. 31C — laws implementing Art. 39(b), (c)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Art. 31C** saves such laws from **Arts. 14, 19**; it was inserted by the **25th Amendment, 1971**.
Option 1 is wrong: estates and agrarian reform belong to **Art. 31A**. Option 2 is wrong: the **Ninth Schedule** goes with **Art. 31B**.
xa: **Art. 31A** saves laws on acquisition of estates, agrarian reform from **Arts. 14, 19** — inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**.
The **Ninth Schedule** was created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
⚠ Kesavananda struck down the part of **Art. 31C** that barred courts from questioning a law declared to give effect to DPSP.

21.s: Following Constitutional amendment Acts were declared as unconstitutional, except
21.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains

21.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court of India in which case?
21.x: Prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine that the Supreme Court first applied in Golaknath (1967). Kesavananda (1973) propounded the basic structure; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art. 368(4),(5); Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs.
21.tq: Golaknath = prospective overruling + FRs transcendental.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied by the Supreme Court in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(2)**.
It is a **judge-made** doctrine, like eclipse, severability and pith and substance.
**Kesavananda (1973)** propounded the **basic structure**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**; **Shankari Prasad (1951)** held Art. 368 includes power to amend FRs.
xa: Golaknath: FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**; an amendment **is** "law" under **Art. 13**.
Bench: **11 judges, 6:5**; it challenged the **17th Amendment**.
Parliament's reply: the **24th Amendment (1971)**, amending **Arts. 13 and 368**.

21.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
21.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
21.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
xs: **Eclipse, severability and pith and substance** are all Supreme Court-made doctrines — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C primacy** came from Parliament's **25th Amendment (1971)**; **unlimited amending power** from the **42nd Amendment**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 each mix in a **Parliament**-made rule.
xa: Other judge-made doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **harmonious construction**, **territorial nexus**.
**Prospective overruling**: Supreme Court — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Basic structure**: Supreme Court — **Kesavananda (1973)**.

21.s: Which of the following originated with Parliament rather than the Supreme Court?
21.x: Art. 13(4) came from Parliament through the 24th Amendment; the other three are Supreme Court doctrines.

21.s: With which basic features is the argument that voting should be raised beyond a statutory right mainly linked?
o: Democracy and free and fair elections as basic features
The primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The basic feature of judicial independence alone
The immunity of all election disputes from judicial review
21.x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.
21.tq: Connect the proposed legal change with the basic constitutional features invoked to support it.
xs: The argument rests on **democracy and free and fair elections as basic features** — option **(1)**.
In the **2026** debate on making **voting a fundamental right**, it was argued voting should be **more than a statutory right**.
xa: **Free and fair elections** were held basic in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**, the **first application** of the doctrine.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also linked **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
Raj Narain struck down the **39th Amendment** clause (**Art. 329A(4)**) putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts.

21.s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense?
o: Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power
The Constitution is written and supreme
21.x: Parliament does not possess an unlimited amending power. The written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federal division of powers and limited amending power restrict parliamentary sovereignty.
21.tq: Find the option that reverses a feature of the limited constitutional system.
xs: The odd one out is "**Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power**" — option **(1)**; its amending power is in fact **limited**.
Real reasons Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**: **written supreme Constitution**, **FRs**, **judicial review**, **federal division** and **limited amending power**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 are genuine reasons, not exceptions.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and non-justiciable.
Basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of courts or Parliament.
The **42nd Amendment** gave Parliament "unlimited amending power" — it was struck down in **Minerva Mills**.

21.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
21.x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
21.tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
xs: The doctrine rests on the **supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts** — option **(4)**.
The judicial review principle **accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts** = supremacy of the **Constitution and the courts** over Parliament (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
As a limit, basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of **Parliament** — so option 1 is the reverse.
xa: Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**.
**Judicial review** is itself basic, so it **cannot be removed even by amendment**.
The doctrine keeps **Art. 368** limited.

21.s: Which Amendment removed the restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts' power to review central laws?
21.x: The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 removed that restriction.
21.tq: Use the amendment sequence to identify the restoring constitutional change.
xs: The **43rd Amendment Act, 1977** removed the bar — option **(2)**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** had barred High Courts from declaring central laws invalid; after the 43rd, **High Courts can** do so.
xa: **Constitutional amendments can** also be challenged on **basic structure** grounds.
⚠ Trap: both "cannot" statements are false (**UPSC 2019**).
The **42nd Amendment**'s Art. 368(4), (5) and widened Art. 31C were struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

21.s: On what does the criticism of the basic structure doctrine as 'judicial rewriting' of the Constitution mainly rest?
o: Absence of any explicit textual definition
21.x: The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case, which is the basis of the criticism.

22.s: Which one of the following propositions was laid down in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?

Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
23.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
23.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
xs: **Constitutional morality** = **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality** — option **(3)**.
It is not the majority's opinion or customary morality.
xa: The phrase is **Ambedkar's, after Grote**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar (2018)**, **Sabarimala (2018)**, **NCT Delhi (2018)**.
Criticism: attacked as **subjective** → route to **judicial overreach**.

23.s: To whom did B.R. Ambedkar refer in using the phrase 'constitutional morality'?
23.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.

**Montesquieu** is linked with **separation of powers**, not this phrase.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Cases: **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi** (all **2018**).
⚠ Criticised as **subjective**.

23.s: Which of the following is a criticism of constitutional morality?
o: It is considered subjective and a possible route to judicial overreach
It makes all Directive Principles directly enforceable
It gives unlimited legislative power to State governments
It prevents courts from referring to constitutional values

It does not make DPSPs enforceable or prevent reference to constitutional values.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi**.

24.s: Which of the following is not an indication of true democracy?
24.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II Screening Test 2017
24.x: Rule by majority alone is not true democracy – a constitutional democracy also needs free and fair elections, respect for the individual and equality before law, and majorities stay bound by constitutional limits.

24.s: In a democracy the powers of the Government are limited by
24.src: APPSC AP Town Planning and Building Overseers 2012
24.x: In a democracy the powers of the government are limited by the Constitution – that is constitutional (limited) government. The people, Parliament and the press act within it.

24.s: "Persons may change but rules should not change" is the principle of
24.x: Constitutional government is government by fixed rules (rule of law), not by the will of persons, so 'persons may change but rules should not change'. A republic, monarchy or socialist system does not carry this meaning.

24.s: A constitutional government by definition is a
24.x: A constitutional government is by definition a limited government – its powers are defined and restricted by the Constitution.

24.s: Constitutional government means
o: a representative government of a nation with the federal structure
a government whose Head enjoys nominal powers
a government whose Head enjoys real powers
a government limited by the terms of the Constitution
24.x: Constitutional government means a government limited by the terms of the Constitution; federal structure and a nominal or real head are not part of the definition.

24.s: Constitutional government means
o: a representative government of a nation with federal
a government whose Head enjoys nominal powers
a government whose Head enjoys real powers
a government limited by the terms of the Constitution
24.x: Constitutional government means a government limited by the terms of the Constitution, which defines and restrains power.

24.s: Constitutional government by definition is a
24.x: A constitutional government is limited by the terms of the Constitution, so it is a limited government.

24.s: In constitutionalism, what is the position of a decision backed by a legislative majority?
24.x: A majoritarian position cannot override constitutionalism; constitutional limits bind even a majority decision.

24.s: The Rule of Law existed in India before PIL through which Articles?
24.x: The rule of law existed before PIL through Articles 14, 32 and 226; PIL widens access to justice but is not indispensable for it.
n: Public Interest Litigation promotes access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Public Interest Litigation strengthens access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

The Rule of Law existed before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law existed through Articles 14, 32, and 226 before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

24.s: What does 'constitutional government' mean?
o: Limited government, limited by the terms of the Constitution
Government by a party with a two-thirds majority
Government in which Parliament is sovereign in every matter
Government run by the civil services
24.x: A constitutional government is a limited government whose powers are fixed and checked by the Constitution.

24.s: Which one of the following factors constitutes the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?
24.x: Separation of powers, with checks and balances among legislature, executive and judiciary, is the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy. Centralisation endangers liberty; an elected government alone is not enough.

24.s: The Presidential Government operates on the Principle of
o: division of powers between Centre and States
24.x: The presidential system rests on separation of powers between executive and legislature; the parliamentary system rests on fusion. Division of powers between Centre and States is federalism.

24.s: Which organ of the government consists of elected representative of people?
24.x: The legislature (Parliament and State Legislatures) consists of the people's elected representatives. The media is not a government organ and judges are appointed.

24.s: According to Montesquieu, what is the most effective means of protecting liberty?
24.x: Montesquieu held that division of powers was the most effective way to protect liberty.
xa: His work: **"The Spirit of Laws" (1748)**; he drew on the **British constitution**.
UPSC 2021 key: best safeguard of liberty = **separation of powers**.
Separation of powers is a **presidential (USA)** principle; India and the UK follow **fusion**.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary and presidential systems?
o: In India the President is the real executive and the Council of Ministers the nominal executive
The principal checks in the US system are checks and balances among the three organs
The parliamentary system rests on fusion of powers
In the USA the President is independent of Congress
24.x: In India the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers the real executive.
xa: Parliamentary checks: **questions**, **confidence/no-confidence votes**.
The USA has a **single real executive**.
⚠ Ambedkar preferred **responsibility over stability**.

24.s: In which of the following does Article 50 of the Constitution direct the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?
o: the public services of the State
24.x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
24.tq: Read the exact constitutional scope of Article 50 instead of expanding it to all institutions.
xs: **Art. 50 (DPSP)**: State shall **separate the judiciary from the executive** in the **public services of the State** — option **(1)**.
It is a Directive Principle, not about Governors, elections or Parliament.
xa: **Judiciary insulated**: Arts. **50, 121, 211, 235** (control of subordinate courts).
**AP angle**: Madras Presidency separated the **Collector's judicial powers** in **1816**.
India has **no rigid separation**; it is **implicit**, not absolute.

24.s: What is the nature of separation of powers in India?
o: Implicit, not absolute, with overlapping functions creating checks and balances
Absolute, as in a pure presidential system
24.x: India has no rigid separation; it is implicit, and overlapping functions create checks and balances.
xa: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: the Constitution does **not** recognise a rigid separation of powers.
**Legislature-executive fusion** under the parliamentary system; **judiciary insulated**.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.

24.s: Which of the following was NOT a consideration behind the framers' choice of the parliamentary system?
o: Familiarity with parliamentary institutions under the Acts of 1919 and 1935
The need to accommodate India's diversity
The desire to avoid American-style executive–legislature conflict
Ambedkar's preference for stability over responsibility
24.x: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability, which is why the parliamentary system was chosen.
xa: Parliamentary system = **fusion** of legislature and executive; ministers must be legislators.
Council of Ministers stays only while it has **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

24.s: In which year was Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of Laws' published?
24.x: Montesquieu set out the division of powers in 'The Spirit of Laws' (1748), drawing on the British constitution.

24.s: The Madras Regulations of 1816, framed under Thomas Munro, did what to the Collector's powers?
o: Vested magisterial and police powers in the Collector again
Separated all judicial powers from the Collector
24.x: Munro's 1816 Regulations reversed the Cornwallis separation by making the Collector also the Magistrate with police control, and gave village heads petty police and judicial powers; separation of the judiciary is now a Directive Principle under Article 50.

24.s: Ambedkar preferred the parliamentary system because it gives priority to which of the following?
24.x: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability, helped by familiarity with the 1919 and 1935 Acts.

24.s: On which country's constitution did Montesquieu mainly draw for his theory of separation of powers?
24.x: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of Laws' (1748) drew on the British constitution.

24.s: In Indian Polity, the executive is subordinate to the-
24.x: In India the executive is subordinate to the legislature: the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)).

24.s: Which Article provides for collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha?
24.x: Article 75(3) provides for the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
24.tq: Match the constitutional provision with the Union-level responsibility rule.
xs: **Article 75(3)** makes the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 164(2)** is the State parallel (Assembly); **Art. 85** = summon/prorogue; **Art. 61** = President's impeachment.
xa: Council stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
**No-confidence motion** — Lok Sabha only.

24.s: In which House can a no-confidence motion for removal of the government be moved?
24.x: A no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha; Question Hour and Zero Hour give day-to-day watch over administration.
xa: **Adjournment** motions also draw attention to lapses.
Financial control: **Budget**, **cut motions**, **PAC** and **Estimates Committees**.
BPSC 2001 key: **executive subordinate to the legislature**.

24.s: Which Article provides for collective responsibility of a State Council of Ministers to the Legislative Assembly?
24.x: Article 164(2) is the State counterpart of Article 75(3), which covers the Union Council of Ministers.

24.s: Which legislative device removes the President of India?
24.x: Impeachment under Article 61 removes the President; a no-confidence motion removes the government.

24.s: In India, to which organ is the executive subordinate?
24.x: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, so the executive is subordinate to the legislature.

24.s: Which of the following pairs (Union – State) is INCORRECTLY matched?
24.x: Collective responsibility is Art. 75(3) for the Union and Art. 164(2) for States, not 163(2).

24.s: When can an ordinance, including one used to alter the legal basis of a judgment, be issued?
o: The legislature is not in session
A National Emergency is in force
24.x: An ordinance is issued when the legislature is not in session; it is subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House.
xa: Criticism: the **ordinance** route is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Union ordinance **Art. 123**; State **Art. 213**.
Other route: **review / curative petition** (**Art. 137**).

24.s: Which Article contains the Governor's ordinance-making power?
24.x: Article 213 covers State ordinances; Article 123 Union ordinances, Article 175 the Governor's addresses and Article 86 the President's addresses.
xa: President's messages also = **Art. 87**; Governor's = **Art. 176**.
Assent: **Art. 111** (President), **Art. 200** (Governor); reservation for President **Art. 201**.
Summon/prorogue: **85 - 174**.

24.s: Under which Article does the Governor summon and prorogue the State Legislature?
24.x: The Governor acts under Article 174 (the President under Article 85); Article 175 is the Governor's address and messages. The gap between sessions cannot exceed six months.
xa: Ordinances: **Art. 123** (Union), **Art. 213** (State).

24.s: Which Article deals with the Governor's assent to Bills passed by the State Legislature?
24.x: Article 200 covers the Governor's assent; Article 111 is presidential assent and Article 201 covers Bills reserved for the President.

24.s: What is the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament under Article 85?
24.x: Article 85 (Article 174 for States) allows at most a six-month gap between sessions.

24.s: Which Articles provide for the President's address and messages to Parliament?
24.x: Articles 86 and 87 cover the President's address and messages; Articles 175 and 176 are the State equivalents.

24.s: Which Article contains the power of the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha?
24.x: Article 85(2) provides for dissolution of the lower House; Article 85(1) deals with summoning.

24.s: What is the status of a law declared ultra vires by the courts in exercise of judicial review?
24.x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action, rests on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and an ultra vires law is void.
xa: **Art. 142** "complete justice" fills gaps — risk of overreach.
**Arts. 122, 212**: courts cannot question legislative proceedings on irregular procedure.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.

24.s: Which Article bars discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge, except on a removal motion?
24.x: Article 121 bars it in Parliament (Article 211 in State Legislatures); Article 122 stops courts questioning parliamentary procedure.

24.s: Article 142 enables the Supreme Court to do which of the following?
o: Prevent all legislative proceedings from judicial scrutiny
Issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Remove a High Court judge without parliamentary procedure
Do complete justice and fill legal gaps in appropriate cases
24.x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice and may allow it to fill legal gaps. Its use can raise concerns about judicial overreach, and its scope is not precisely defined.
24.tq: Apply the constitutional power to a legal-gap situation rather than confusing it with ordinance or removal powers.
xs: **Art. 142** lets the SC do **"complete justice"** and **fill gaps** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Vishaka** guidelines before the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Ordinances are issued by the executive (**Art. 123/213**), not the Court.
xa: Risk: **overreach**; scope **undefined**.
Frequent **Art. 142** use is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Judicial review rests on Arts. **13, 32, 226**.

24.s: On which Articles does judicial review of laws and executive action in India mainly rest?
24.x: Judicial review rests on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and a law found ultra vires is void.

24.s: Which Articles bar courts from questioning the proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures on the ground of irregular procedure?
24.x: Articles 122 and 212 protect legislative proceedings from court inquiry on procedure; 121 and 211 bar discussion of judges.

24.s: In which case was the 42nd Amendment's bar on judicial review struck down?
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
24.x: Minerva Mills struck down the bar; Raj Narain struck down the 39th Amendment's validation of the PM's election, and Golaknath predates the 42nd Amendment.
xa: Raj Narain: the legislature **cannot decide an election dispute** — a judicial function.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers a **basic feature**.

24.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers?
o: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
24.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) held there is no rigid separation of powers and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about separation of powers in India?
o: Kesavananda Bharati recognised separation of powers as a basic feature
Raj Narain held that the legislature could finally decide an election dispute
Raj Narain was connected with the challenge to the 39th Amendment
Deciding an election dispute is a judicial function
24.x: Raj Narain held the legislature cannot decide an election dispute because it is a judicial function.
xa: **Minerva Mills**: the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review struck down.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: no rigid separation of powers.

24.s: Which Amendment placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule?
24.x: The 76th Amendment did so; after I.R. Coelho, such post-24 April 1973 entries can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
xa: Override routes are all tested against the **basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.
**24th Amendment** overrode **Golaknath**.

24.s: Which Amendment's validation of the PM's election was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)?
24.x: Raj Narain held the legislature cannot decide an election dispute and struck down the 39th Amendment's validation.

24.s: In which case was separation of powers held to be a basic feature of the Constitution?
24.x: Kesavananda (1973) treated separation of powers as a basic feature; Ram Jawaya Kapur only held there is no rigid separation.

24.s: Under I.R. Coelho, Ninth Schedule entries made after which date are open to judicial review?
24.x: I.R. Coelho made laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 reviewable.

24.s: The 77th Constitutional Amendment (promotion quota) followed which judgment?
24.x: The 77th followed Indra Sawhney; the 24th followed Golaknath, the 26th Madhav Rao and the 1st Champakam Dorairajan.
xa: **Limit**: every override is tested against the **basic structure**.
Exam angle: Parliament **cannot** overrule a judgment by a **simple resolution**.
**76th Amdt** placed the TN **69%** quota in the Ninth Schedule.

24.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Advisory opinion to the President – Article 137
Advice under Article 143 – Binding on the President
Supreme Court review of its own judgment – Article 137
Supreme Court review of its own judgment – Article 143
24.x: The Supreme Court reviews its own judgments under Article 137; the President seeks its advice under Article 143, and that advice is not binding.

24.s: How can Parliament override a judicial judgment?
o: Changing the law or constitutional basis underlying it
A resolution of a joint sitting
24.x: Parliament can override a judgment only by changing its legal or constitutional basis, subject to the basic structure; a simple resolution cannot do it.
xa: Examples: **24th** (Golaknath), **26th** (privy purses), **77th** (Indra Sawhney).
A validating law cannot **decide the dispute itself**.
**Raj Narain** struck down the **39th Amendment**'s validation of the PM's election.

24.s: The One Nation One Election Bill, as described in the context of electoral synchronisation, proposes amendments to which of the following Articles?
24.x: The One Nation One Election Bill is associated with amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327. Critics argue that fixed tenure may weaken collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.
24.tq: Use article-number discrimination and avoid substituting the related collective-responsibility provisions.
xs: The **One Nation One Election Bill** amends **Arts. 83, 172, 327** — option **(1)**.
Critics: **fixed tenure** weakens **collective responsibility** under **Arts. 75, 164** — these are not the amended Articles.
xa: Collective responsibility: **Art. 75(3)** (Union), **Art. 164(2)** (States).
SC: **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.
Council of Ministers stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

24.s: Which Constitutional Amendment overrode the Golaknath judgment?
24.x: The 24th overrode Golaknath; the 1st overrode Champakam Dorairajan, the 26th Madhav Rao and the 77th Indra Sawhney.

24.s: Which judgment did the 26th Amendment, abolishing privy purses, override?
24.x: The 26th Amendment overrode Madhav Rao (privy purses).

24.s:
Consider the following statements about overriding a judgment:
1. A validating law must remove the basis of the judgment.
2. A validating law may simply declare a judgment void.
3. Advice given under Article 143 is not binding on the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: a validating law cannot simply declare a judgment void.

24.s: Absolute Sovereign power of the Monarch was advocated by
24.x: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) advocated the absolute sovereign power of the monarch, since people surrender all rights to the sovereign. Locke favoured limited government and Rousseau popular sovereignty.

24.s: Who among the following is the author of the book, The Social Contract?
24.x: The Social Contract (1762) was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Hobbes wrote Leviathan, Locke Two Treatises of Government.

24.s: Who among the following supports customary rights?
24.x: D.G. Ritchie is an exponent of the historical (customary) theory of rights – rights grow out of custom. Locke stands for natural rights.

24.s: The state is a necessary evil according to
24.x: Individualists see the State as a necessary evil, to be kept minimal; anarchists want it abolished, so they are not the answer.

24.s: The concept of "National rights" was emphasised by
24.x: 'National rights' is a misprint for natural rights: John Locke made the natural rights of life, liberty and property the basis of government; Dalton, Leacock and Bryce did not.

24.s: Who among the following proposed the theory of 'Civil Legitimacy'?
24.x: Unkeyed: 'civil legitimacy' is not a standard theory name. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau all grounded the legitimacy of civil government in a social contract, and no source attributes the phrase to one of them, so no option can be fixed.

25.s: Which Article of the Indian Constitution discusses the election of the President?

25.s: Articles 54 & 55 of Indian Constitution deal with
25.src: APPSC Assistant Directors in AP Economic & Statistics 2012
25.x: Articles 54 and 55 deal with the election of the President (electoral college and manner of election); the VP's election is Art. 66.

25.s: With reference to the election of the President of India, who among the following is NOT included in the electoral college for the election of the President of India?
o: The elected members of the legislative assemblies of the states
The elected members of the legislative assemblies of the Union Territories
The elected members of Legislative council of states
The elected members of both the Houses of Parliament
25.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
25.x: Members of State Legislative Councils, elected or nominated, are not in the President's electoral college; elected MPs and elected MLAs (including Delhi and Puducherry) are.

25.s: The President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of
o: All the members of both the Houses of Parliament and all the members of all the Legislative Assemblies
All the elected members of both the Houses of Parliament and all the members of all the Legislative Assemblies
All the members of both the Houses of Parliament and all the elected members of all the Legislative Assemblies
All the elected members of both the Houses of Parliament and all the elected members of all the Legislative Assemblies

25.x: Only elected members vote: elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs of the Assemblies; nominated members are excluded.

25.s: The Constitution of India provides that the President shall be elected:
o: by open voting by the members of the electoral college
directly by the people of India
in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of single transferable vote and the voting at such election shall be by secret ballot
by majority of votes of the members of the electoral college present and voting in the capital of India

25.x: Art. 55(3): election by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and voting by secret ballot.

25.s:
With reference to the election of the president of India, consider the following statements:

A. The value of the vote of each MLA varies from State to state.

B. The value of the vote of MPs of the Lok Sabha is more than the value of the vote of MPs of the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
25.x: A is correct: an MLA's vote value depends on the State's population and seats, so it varies. B is wrong: every elected MP, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, has the same vote value.

25.s: If the election of a person as president is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in exercise of the power and duties, on or before the date of the decision of the supreme Court shall be
o: Parliament has to reapprove the actions
Newly elected president may once again ratify the actions
25.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
25.x: Art. 71(2): acts done by the President before the Supreme Court declares his election void are not invalidated. (No printed key.)

25.s: The name of the candidate for the office of the president of India has to be proposed by
o: any 5 members of the electoral college
any 50 members of the electoral college
25.x: The nomination must be subscribed by at least 50 electors of the electoral college as proposers and 50 as seconders (since 1997).

25.s:
The President is elected by an Electoral College (3) consisting of:
A. Elected members of both Houses of Parliament. 96. As p
B. Nominated members of both Houses of (4) Parliament. nu Mi C.The elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of all the States.
D. Nominated members of the Legislative Assemblies of all the States.
E. The elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of NCT of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry.
o: A, B, C, D and E
25.x: The electoral college is A (elected MPs), C (elected MLAs of States) and E (elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry, 70th Amendment); nominated members (B, D) are excluded.

25.s: Which one of the following is part of the electoral college for the election of the President of India but does not form part of the forum for his impeachment?
25.x: State Legislative Assemblies (elected MLAs) vote in the election but impeachment is done by Parliament alone; Legislative Councils have no part in either.

25.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. If the election of the President of India is declared void by the Supreme Court of India, all acts done by him/her in the performance of duties of his/her office of President before the date of decision become invalid.
2. Election for the post of the President of India can be postponed on the ground that some Legislative Assemblies have been dissolved, and elections are yet to take place.
3. When a Bill is presented to the President of India, the Constitution prescribes time limits within which he/she has to declare his/her assent.
How many of the above statements are correct?
25.x: All three are wrong: acts before the election is voided stay valid; the election cannot be postponed because some Assemblies are dissolved (Art. 71(4)); the Constitution fixes no time limit for assent. The 2025 Presidential Reference also refused judicial timelines.

25.s:
Consider the following statements in respect of election to the President of India:
1. The members nominated to either House of the Parliament or the Legislative Assemblies of States are also eligible to be included in the Electoral College.
2. Higher the number of elective Assembly seats, higher is the value of vote of each MLA of that State.
3. The value of vote of each MLA of Madhya Pradesh is greater than that of Kerala.
4. The value of vote of each MLA of Puducherry is higher than that of Arunachal Pradesh because the ratio of total population to total number of elective seats in Puducherry is greater as compared to Arunachal Pradesh.
How many of the above statements are correct?
25.x: Only statement 4 is correct (Puducherry 16 vs Arunachal 8, because its population per seat is higher). 1 is wrong (nominated members are out), 2 is wrong (value depends on population per seat), 3 is wrong (MP 131 < Kerala 152).

25.s: Who among the following are not included in the Electoral College for the election of the President of India?
o: Elected members of the House of the People
Elected members of the Council of States
Elected member of the Legislative Assemblies of the States
Elected members of the Legislative Councils of the States
25.x: Members of the State Legislative Councils are not in the electoral college; elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs are.

25.s: Which one of the following is electoral college for the President but not forum for his impeachment?
25.x: Elected MLAs of the State Legislative Assemblies elect the President but impeachment (Art. 61) is by Parliament alone.

25.s: How is the President elected in India?
25.x: The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs, not directly or by one House.

25.s: In India, the President is elected by

26.s:
In connection with the veto power of the Indian President, which one of the following statement/statements is/are valid?

I. The Indian President possesses 'Suspensive Veto' in the case of Money Bills but not in the case of Finance Bills.

II. The Indian President can exercise 'Absolute Veto' with respect to the Government Bills at all times.

III. The Indian President enjoys 'Pocket Veto' indefinitely whereas the American President possesses 'Qualified Veto'.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
26.src: APPSC Group-I Prelims Paper-I Screening Test 2024
26.x: Only III is valid: the President holds the pocket veto without time limit while the US President has a qualified veto. I reverses the rule (no suspensive veto on Money Bills), II is wrong (absolute veto on Government Bills only when the Cabinet resigns), and IV is not the object – the veto exists to prevent hasty or unconstitutional legislation.

26.s: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution, the President of India enjoys the power to withhold his assent to any Bill passed by both the Houses of the Parliament?
26.x: Article 111 lets the President assent, withhold assent or return a non-Money Bill passed by both Houses; Art. 108 is the joint sitting, Art. 109 Money Bill procedure and Art. 63 the Vice-President.

26.s: In pocket veto, the President of India can keep a bill for how much duration?
26.x: In a pocket veto the President neither assents, rejects nor returns the Bill; Art. 111 prescribes no time limit, so he can hold it for an indefinite period.

26.s: Does the President of India have veto power?
o: The constitution is silent on this
26.x: Yes – the Indian President has the absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes; he lacks only the qualified veto.

26.s: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Veto Power of the President of India.
o: He cannot return a Money Bill passed by the Parliament.
He has no Veto Power over Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368.
He has no Veto Power over an Ordinary Bill passed for second time by the Parliament.
He cannot Veto a Money Bill passed by the State Legislature duly forwarded by the Governor of a State.
26.x: (d) is wrong: for a State Money Bill reserved by the Governor, the President may assent or withhold assent, so he can veto it. The others are right – a Money Bill cannot be returned, an amendment Bill must be signed (24th Amendment) and a re-passed ordinary Bill must be assented to.

26.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pocket veto of the President of India?
o: As in the USA, the President must decide within 10 days, failing which the Bill becomes law.

Under it, the President neither assents to, nor rejects, nor returns the Bill.
President Giani Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
26.x: The 10-day limit is a US feature; Article 111 sets no time limit in India, which is what makes the pocket veto possible.
xa: Only Union instance: **Zail Singh (1986)**, **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill**.
The **Governor** has **no** pocket veto.

26.s: To which Bills does the suspensive veto of the President apply?
26.x: The suspensive veto (return once) applies only to Ordinary Bills, not Money Bills.

26.s: To which Bills is the absolute veto of the President usually applied?
26.x: The absolute veto is used for private members' Bills and for Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.

26.s: Where is the rule that a Bill becomes law if not decided within 10 days found?
26.x: The 10-day rule is a US feature; Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the Indian President.

26.s: What can the President do with a Money Bill passed by Parliament?

Keep it pending only for ten days

**Pocket veto** is possible because **Art. 111** prescribes **no time limit**.

26.s: To Financial Bills of which category can the President's one-time power to return a Bill apply?
26.x: The one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II; Money Bills cannot be returned.

26.s: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limitations as which of the following?

An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance has the same effect as an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]

27.s: Chairman of Rajya Sabha is-
o: The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
27.x: The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Arts. 64, 89(1)); the CJI, CEC and PM are not.

27.s:
The Vice-President of India :
1. Is the second highest dignitary of India.
2. Has no formal function attached to his office
3. Discharges the functions of the President during his absence.
4. Acts as the President if the President resigns, or is removed or dies.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
27.x: 1, 3 and 4: the VP is the second-highest dignitary, discharges the President's functions in his absence and acts as President on a vacancy. Statement 2 is wrong – he has the formal function of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

27.s: Which one of the following is Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
o: The person elected to this post/office

27.s: Which one of the following is not appointed by the President of India:
27.x: The Vice-President is elected by MPs of both Houses (Art. 66); the PM (Art. 75), Governor (Art. 155) and CEC (Art. 324) are appointed by the President.

27.s: The Chairman of Council of States (Rajya Sabha) is
o: Elected by members of State Council
27.x: Article 89(1): the Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States; he is not appointed by the President or separately elected as Chairman.

27.s: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is
o: nominated by the President of India
nominated by the Vice-President of India
27.x: Articles 64 and 89(1) make the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. He is elected, not nominated by the President, and the Leader of Opposition does not chair the House.

27.s: How is Vice-President of India elected?
o: through direct election by the MPs of Lok Sabha and
through election by the MPs of Lok Sabha and Rajya
27.x: The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of the members of both Houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) of Parliament (Art. 66(1)) – not directly or by nomination.

27.s:
Who amongst the following elects the Vice-President of India?
Select the correct answer from the code given below:
1. Member of Lok Sabha
2. Members of Rajya Sabha
3. Members of Legislative Assemblies
4. Members of Legislative Councils
27.x: Only members of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha elect the Vice-President; State Legislative Assemblies and Councils have no role (unlike the President's election).

27.s: Who elect the Vice President of India?
27.x: The Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses of Parliament (elected and nominated) by PR-STV; State Legislatures do not take part.

27.s: Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
27.x: The Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice-President as its ex-officio Chairman, though he is not a member of the House.

27.s: Who presides over the sessions of Rajya Sabha
27.x: The Vice-President, as ex-officio Chairman, presides over the Rajya Sabha; the Speaker and Deputy Speaker preside over the Lok Sabha.

27.s: According to the Indian Constitution, the Vice-President must have the qualifications for election to which of the following?
o: Neither Lok Sabha nor Rajya Sabha
Both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
27.x: Article 66(3): the Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha (the President – of the Lok Sabha).

27.s: Who among the following form the electoral college that elects the Vice-President of India?
o: elected members of both Houses of Parliament only
elected MPs and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
all members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
all MPs and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
27.x: All MPs, elected and nominated, vote by PR-STV and secret ballot; State legislatures have no role in the Vice-President's election.
xa: Size of the electoral college = all MPs, **788** (**543 LS + 245 RS**) when both Houses are full.
The election is conducted by the **ECI** under the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.
⚠ Nominated MPs **vote** for the VP; State MLAs do **not**.
A removal resolution against the VP can first be moved **only in the Rajya Sabha**.

27.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment and the 44th Constitutional Amendment had what effect on Presidential election disputes?
o: The 39th Amendment vested the disputes in Parliament and the 44th retained that arrangement
The 39th Amendment removed the Supreme Court’s power and the 44th Amendment restored it
The 39th Amendment created the power and the 44th Amendment abolished it
Both Amendments transferred the power to the Election Commission
27.x: The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
27.tq: Link each Amendment to its opposite constitutional effect instead of relying on the later amendment alone.
xs: The **39th Amendment (1975)** removed the **Supreme Court's** power over these election disputes and the **44th Amendment (1978)** restored it — so option **(2)** is correct.
The power was never vested in the **Election Commission**, and the 44th did not abolish or retain a parliamentary forum.
xa: The 39th Amendment covered disputes on elections of the **President, VP, PM and Speaker**.
Today the forum is the **Supreme Court** under **Art 71**.
**Acts done before** the SC voids an election remain valid.

27.s: Which Article makes the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
27.x: Article 64 makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman; 63 creates the office, 66 covers election and 67 the term.
n: Article 63 provides for a Vice-President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Article 64. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The term of office of the Vice-President is five years under Article 67. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Article 69:** VP's **oath**, administered by the **President**.
**Article 71:** election disputes decided by the **Supreme Court** — final.
**Article 65:** VP **acts as President** during a vacancy, for at most **six months**.
⚠ **Article 68:** vacancy election "as soon as possible", **no deadline** — unlike the President's **6 months** (Art 62).

27.s: On which office is the office of the Vice-President of India modelled?
o: Deputy Prime Minister of the UK
27.x: The Indian Vice-President's office is modelled on the American Vice-President.
n: The Vice-President holds the second-highest constitutional office after the President in the Order of Precedence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The office of the Vice-President is modelled on the American Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan** was also the **longest-serving** VP — **two** terms (**1952-62**).
**Mohammad Hamid Ansari:** only VP to serve **two full terms** (**2007-17**).
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first VP; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present VP (**2025**).

27.s: The Vice-President of India is ex officio President of which of the following bodies?
27.x: The Vice-President is also the ex-officio President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA).
27.tq: Use the exact institutional title to distinguish ICWA from other national bodies.
xs: The VP is ex officio **President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His other ex-officio role is **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (**Art. 64**).
xa: VP qualifications: **citizen**, **35 years**, eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha**.
Electoral college: **members of both Houses**, elected **and nominated**, by **PR-STV**.
⚠ The VP holds **no other office of profit**, but ex-officio posts like these are part of the office.

27.s: When both Houses are full, the electoral college for the Vice-President has how many members?
27.x: All 788 MPs, elected and nominated, elect the Vice-President; State Legislatures have no role.

27.x: Under Article 71 all disputes over the Vice-President's election are decided finally by the Supreme Court.

27.s: Which of the following is NOT a part of the Parliament of India under Article 79?
27.x: Article 79: Parliament = President + Council of States + House of the People; the VP chairs the RS but is not a member or part of Parliament.

27.s: By which system is the Vice-President of India elected?
o: First-past-the-post system by members of the Lok Sabha
Proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot
Open ballot by simple majority of both Houses
27.x: The Vice-President is elected by MPs of both Houses through PR-STV, and voting is by secret ballot.

27.s: Under which Act are the elections to the offices of President and Vice-President of India held?
27.x: The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 governs these elections.

27.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides that there shall be a Vice-President of India?
27.x: Article 63 creates the office of Vice-President; Article 64 makes him ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT a qualification for election as Vice-President of India?
o: Qualification for election as a member of the Lok Sabha
Qualification for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: The Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha. Qualification for election to the Lok Sabha is not the prescribed condition.
27.tq: Find the one swapped constitutional qualification among closely related House requirements.
xs: Qualification for election to the **Lok Sabha** is NOT a VP qualification — so option **(2)** is correct.
The VP must be a **citizen**, aged **35 years**, and eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha** — options (1), (3), (4) are real qualifications.
⚠ Lok Sabha eligibility is the **President's** qualification; the VP's is **Rajya Sabha** eligibility.
xa: **Art. 64:** the VP is **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** but is **not a member** of the RS.
The VP holds **no other office of profit**.
**Art. 63** simply says there shall be a Vice-President.

27.s: Which of the following statements about the Vice President of India are correct? i. The Vice President is elected for five years. ii. The Vice President acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. iii. The Vice President acts as the President only until a new President is elected.
27.x: All three: the VP is elected for five years, is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and on a vacancy acts as President only until a new President is elected (max six months).

27.s: Which of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the office of Vice-President?
o: The Vice-President office is modelled on the lines of the American Vice-President.
The Vice-President is elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament.
All doubts and disputes in connection with the election of the Vice-President are inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court of India.

If the office of the Vice-President falls vacant due to resignation, removal, death, or any other reason, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha acts as Vice-President until a new Vice-President is elected.
27.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
27.x: Not correct: (d). The Constitution is silent on who acts as Vice-President in a vacancy; the Deputy Chairman only performs the Chairman's duties in the Rajya Sabha. (a)-(c) are true – the office is modelled on the American VP, elected by both Houses, disputes go to the SC.

27.s: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Vice President of India.
o: Vice President cannot act as Chairperson of Rajya Sabha while he is officiating as President of India.
Vice President of India can be removed by a 2/3rd majority in Rajya Sabha and simple majority in Lok Sabha.
As Chairperson of Rajya Sabha, he has a Casting Vote.
The election disputes of Vice President of India are decided by the Supreme Court
27.x: Wrong: (b). The VP is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its then members (effective majority) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha – not two-thirds. He does not chair the RS while acting as President, has a casting vote, and the SC decides his election disputes.

27.s: In case of the office of President of India falls vacant, the new President is to be elected within ____ months of the vacancy.
27.x: Article 62(2): an election to fill a vacancy in the President's office must be held within six months of the vacancy; meanwhile the VP acts as President.

27.s: The Vice President of India can submit his resignation letter to
27.x: Under Article 67(a) the Vice-President resigns by writing addressed to the President – not the PM or Parliament.

27.s: In case a president dies while in office, the vice-president can act as president for a maximum period of
27.x: On the President's death the VP acts as President only until a new President is elected, which must be within six months (Art. 62) – not for the remaining term.

27.s: The President of India may resign his office by writing under his hand a letter of resignation addressed to the
27.x: Article 56(1)(a): the President resigns by writing addressed to the Vice-President, who informs the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

27.s: According to Article 67, the resolution for removing the Vice-President of India can be moved first only in
o: Either of the two Houses of the Parliament
Joint sitting of the two Houses of the Parliament
27.x: Article 67(b): the resolution to remove the VP can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha, after 14 days' notice, and must then be agreed to by the Lok Sabha.

27.s: Who among the following administers oath of the office and secrecy to the Vice-President of India?
27.x: Under Article 69 the oath of office is administered to the Vice-President by the President (or a person appointed by him), not by the CJI, PM or Speaker.

27.s: The procedure for the removal of Vice-President is given in which Article of Indian Constitution?
27.x: Article 67(b) provides for removal of the Vice-President. Article 56 concerns the President's term and resignation, Article 60 the President's oath, and Article 77 the conduct of Government business.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vice-President of India.

I. The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college consisting of all the members of the Both Houses of the Parliament.

II. The Constitution is silent about a person who is having the duties of the Vice-President during the period of vacancy.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
27.x: Both: the VP is elected by all members of both Houses, and the Constitution names no one to discharge the VP's duties during a vacancy (Art. 68 only says it is filled as soon as possible).

27.s: The Vice-President may be removed from his office by a resolution of –
27.x: Article 67(b): the Vice-President is removed by a resolution of the Council of States passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by the House of the People; the Cabinet has no role.

27.s: The resolution for removing the Vice‑President of India can be moved in the:
27.x: The removal resolution can be initiated only in the Rajya Sabha (majority of all its members) and then needs the Lok Sabha's agreement – not in the Lok Sabha, either House or a joint sitting.

27.s: If Vice-President of India has to discharge the duties of President of India in his absence due to some reasons, then what is/are true for such duration? (i) In this duration, Vice-President holds the post of Chairman of Council of States (ii) In this duration, Vice-President will get the emolument of President (iii) If in this duration, Vice-President resigns, then Chief Justice of India will perform the duties of President of India
27.x:
Most books and keys: (ii) and (iii). Strictly, the Art. 64 proviso only bars him from performing the Chairman's duties while acting – he is not removed from the post of Chairman.
(ii) and (iii): while discharging the President's functions the VP draws the President's emoluments and does not perform the Chairman's duties (the Deputy Chairman presides); if he resigns, both offices are vacant and the CJI discharges the President's functions under the 1969 Act.

27.s: A resolution for the removal of the Vice-President of India can be proposed in –
27.x: Under Art 67(b) the removal resolution is moved only in the Rajya Sabha, then needs the Lok Sabha's agreement; it is not moved in the Lok Sabha or a joint sitting.

27.s: If the Vice-President of India wishes to resign from his office, who should he address his resignation to?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Dy. Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: Art. 67(a): the Vice-President resigns by writing addressed to the President.

27.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Tie in the Rajya Sabha – Vice-President has no vote
Resolution for his own removal – Vice-President presides
Re-election of the Vice-President – any number of times
Vote of the Vice-President – on every motion in the first instance
27.x: The Vice-President can be re-elected any number of times. He has only a casting vote in a tie and does not preside while his own removal is considered.
n: The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President presides over the sittings of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President has a casting vote in case of a tie in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President does not preside when a resolution for the Vice-President’s removal is under consideration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]

27.s: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice-President of India?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most judge of the Supreme Court
27.x: Under Article 69 the President administers the Vice-President's oath; the CJI administers the President's oath.
xa: The VP is **re-eligible any number of times**.
Removal resolution: **only in the RS**, by **effective majority**; LS agrees by **simple majority**; **no grounds** stated.
Resignation is addressed to the **President** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately.

27.s: While the Vice-President acts as President, who presides over the Rajya Sabha?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: While acting as President under Article 65, the Vice-President stops doing the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and the Deputy Chairman presides.

27.s: To whom does the Vice-President of India address his resignation?
27.x: Under Article 67(a) the Vice-President resigns by writing to the President, and the resignation takes effect immediately. The President resigns to the Vice-President; the CJI administers the President's oath; the Speaker is informed of the President's resignation; the Prime Minister receives no constitutional resignation of either office.
27.tq: President resigns to VP; VP resigns to President.
xs: The VP resigns by writing to the **President of India** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The **President** resigns to the **Vice-President** — the reverse pair is a common trap.
xa: The VP's **oath** is administered by the **President** (**Art 69**).
**Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned on health grounds under **Art 67(a)** in **July 2025**.
Term: **5 years**, re-eligible **any number of times**.

27.s: Within what time must a vacancy in the office of the Vice-President of India be filled?
o: Within six months of the vacancy in every case
As soon as possible, without a constitutionally prescribed six-month deadline
Within one year, after approval by the Supreme Court
Only at the next general election to the Lok Sabha
27.x: Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible. Unlike the vacancy in the office of President, no six-month deadline is prescribed for this election.
27.tq: Compare the vacancy rules for President and Vice-President, especially the presence or absence of a fixed deadline.
xs: A VP vacancy is filled **"as soon as possible"**, with **no deadline** (**Art 68**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **six-month** limit applies to a **President's** vacancy (**Art 62**), not the VP's.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned in **July 2025** — the **third mid-term vacancy** after **V.V. Giri (1969)** and **Krishan Kant (2002)**.
**C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected after that vacancy (**September 2025**).
The VP continues in office till the successor takes charge (**Art 67(c)**).

27.s: What is the maximum period for which the Vice-President may act as President when the office of President falls vacant or the President is unable to discharge functions?
27.x: The Vice-President can act as President for at most six months, within which a new President must be elected.
27.tq: Recall the six-month limit.
n: The maximum period for which the Vice-President acts as President is six months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
An election for a new President must be held within six months when the Vice-President acts as President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President acts as President under Article 65 when the office of the President falls vacant. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President acts as President when the President is unable to discharge the President’s functions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xs: The VP can act as President for a maximum of **six months** — option **(1)**.
A new President must be **elected within six months** of the vacancy (**Article 65** context; Art 62).
He acts on **death, resignation, removal**, or when the President is **unable to discharge functions** (absence, illness).
xa: While acting as President he **ceases to be RS Chairman** → the **Deputy Chairman** presides.
He draws the **President's salary, allowances and privileges**, not the Chairman's.
As Chairman of the RS his salary is **not charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.

27.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the removal of the Vice-President of India?
o: The resolution must originate in the Rajya Sabha.

27.x: The Constitution does not state any grounds for removing the Vice-President; the other three statements describe the procedure correctly.
xa: **14 days' notice** is needed before the resolution is moved.
⚠ The President is removed by **impeachment** (**Art 61**), in **either House**, by **2/3**.
"Where can the removal resolution first be moved" → **Rajya Sabha** is a stock exam angle.

27.s: What is the minimum notice required before a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President can be moved?

27.x: Article 56(2) requires the Vice-President to communicate the President's resignation at once to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
