A Money Bill requires the President’s recommendation before introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: Also not money bills: **fees for licences or services**, taxes by **local bodies** for local purposes.
**Joint Sitting** is **not** possible for a Money Bill.

33.s: Which one of the following is included within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1) of the Constitution?
o: Fees for licences issued by local authorities
Taxes imposed by a municipality for local purposes
Imposition of fines by a criminal court
Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
33.x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax. Fines, licence fees and local taxes are not, by themselves, matters of a Money Bill.
33.tq: Identify the exact constitutional subject instead of selecting nearby revenue-related terms.
xs: **Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax** is an **Art. 110(1)** matter — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Fines/penalties**, **fees for licences**, and **taxes by local bodies for local purposes** are not money-bill matters — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Other Art. 110(1) matters: **borrowing by GoI**; custody of the **Consolidated/Contingency Fund**.
Also: appropriation from the **CFI** and declaring expenditure **charged**.
A Money Bill deals **only** with Art. 110(1) matters.

33.s: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha?
33.x: The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations; otherwise it is deemed passed by both Houses.

33.s: Which case upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while the Money-Bill issue was subsequently referred to a larger bench in another case?
33.x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a Money Bill in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018). The Money-Bill question was later referred to a seven-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019).
33.tq: Anchor the judicial developments by matching the case names with their years and sequence.
xs: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2018)** upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill; **Rojer Mathew (2019)** referred the question to a larger bench — so option **(1)** is correct.
Options (2) and (3) swap the years.
xa: Rojer Mathew referred it to a **7-judge** bench.
The **Speaker's** certificate on a Money Bill is **final** under **Art. 110(3)**.
A Money Bill deals **only** with **Art. 110(1)** matters.

33.s: Under Article 110(3), who decides finally whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
33.x: The Speaker's decision is final, and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
xa: The Rajya Sabha must return it within **14 days**, with or without recommendations.
The President may assent or withhold but **cannot return** it.
The **Finance Bill** is usually certified a Money Bill.

33.s: In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Money Bill question was referred to a larger bench of how many judges?
33.x: Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the Money Bill question to a larger 7-judge bench.

33.s: Under Article 110(2), a Bill is NOT a Money Bill merely because it provides for taxes imposed by whom?
33.x: Taxes by local bodies for local purposes, fines and licence fees do not make a Bill a Money Bill.

33.s: The Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill is endorsed when the Bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha and to whom?
33.x: The certificate is endorsed when the Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha (Art. 109) and to the President (Art. 111).

33.s: What happens if the Rajya Sabha does not return the Appropriation Bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days?
o: It is deemed to have been passed by both Houses
It goes back to the President
33.x: The Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill. If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.

33.s: In which House, by whom and on whose recommendation can a Money Bill be introduced?
o: In either House by any member with the Speaker's consent
In the Rajya Sabha by a minister on the President's recommendation
In the Lok Sabha by a private member with the Rajya Sabha's approval
In the Lok Sabha by a minister on the President's recommendation
33.x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, and only on the President's recommendation.
xa: The Rajya Sabha must return it within **14 days** (**Art. 109**).
**No joint sitting** on a Money Bill.

33.s: What can the Rajya Sabha do with the Annual Financial Statement?
o: Vote on the Demands for Grants
Discuss it but not vote on the Demands for Grants
33.x: The Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement, but voting on Demands for Grants (Art. 113) is only in the Lok Sabha.

33.s: Demands for Grants are provided for under which Article?
33.x: Article 113 deals with Demands for Grants; 112 is the Annual Financial Statement, 114 the Appropriation Bill and 116 the vote on account.

33.s: Whose assent is necessary to introduce bill for the creation of new states?
33.src: APPSC Fisheries Development Officer, Assistant Inspector of
33.x: Under Art. 3 a Bill for new States or altering boundaries or names needs the President's recommendation before introduction.

33.s: Which article in the Constitution of India provides Special provisions as to Financial Bills?
33.x: Article 117 contains the special provisions as to Financial Bills; Art. 323 is reports of PSCs, 37 DPSP enforceability, 247 additional courts.

33.s: Identify the wrong statement with regard to a bill meant for creating a new state
o: The bill requires previous sanction of the President for its introduction in the Parliament
The bill must be first introduced in Rajya Sabha
The bill requires simple majority in both the houses of Parliament
The bill does not come under Article 368
33.x: A Bill to create a new State needs the President's recommendation, a simple majority and is not an Art. 368 amendment – but it can be introduced in either House, so 'must first be introduced in the RS' is wrong.

33.s: Which one of the following is not Constitutional Prerogative of the President of India?
o: Returning an ordinary Bill for reconsideration
Returning a financial bill for reconsideration
33.x:
Most books and keys: returning a financial (Money) Bill. Strictly, Financial Bills I and II under Art. 117 can be returned like ordinary Bills (Laxmikanth); only a Money Bill cannot.
Exam keys read 'financial bill' here as the Finance/Money Bill, which the President cannot return; returning ordinary Bills, dissolving the LS and appointing the PM are his prerogatives.

33.s: To which of the following Bills the President must accord his Sanction without sending it back for fresh consideration?
o: Bill seeking Amendment to the constitution
Bills passed by both the houses of the Parliament
33.x:
Most books and keys: Finance (Money) Bills. Strictly, only a Constitution Amendment Bill must be assented to (Art. 368(2), 24th Amendment 1971); a Money Bill cannot be returned but assent can be withheld.
A Finance (Money) Bill cannot be sent back for reconsideration – the President may only assent (or, in theory, withhold); ordinary Bills can be returned once.

33.s: Rajya Sabha can delay the Finance Bill sent for its consideration by Lok Sabha for a maximum period of-
33.x: Exam keys treat the Finance Bill as a Money Bill, which the Rajya Sabha can hold for at most fourteen days.

33.s: A Bill which merely involves expenditure and does not include any of the matters specified in Article 110 can be:
o: Initiated in either House of Parliament
Initiated only in joint session of both House of
33.x: A Bill merely involving expenditure (Financial Bill II, Art. 117(3)) can be initiated in either House; only its consideration needs the President's recommendation.

33.s: Which of the following is not correct? i. Each money bill is finance bill. ii. Each finance bill is not a money bill. iii. Finance bill can be introduced in Lok Sabha only. iv. Finance bill is presigned by the President. v. Rajya Sabha can detain the finance bill for 14 days. vi. President can not refuse to sign on finance bill. vii. Rajya Sabha can amend the finance bill. viii.On deadlock on finance bill joint session can be called.
33.x: i-iv hold (every Money Bill is a Finance Bill; Finance Bills start in the LS on the President's recommendation); v and vi are wrong because a (non-money) Financial Bill is passed like an ordinary Bill – the RS has no 14-day limit and the President can refuse assent; vii and viii are right.

33.s: The provision that “no bill imposing tax can be introduced in the Legislature except on the recommendation of the President” is covered in the Constitution of India under-
33.x: Art. 117(1): a Bill imposing any tax shall not be introduced or moved except on the President's recommendation. Arts. 266, 306, 307 are unrelated.

33.s: Special provision regarding Financial Bills is given under-
33.x: Article 117 is the special provision as to Financial Bills; Art. 119 regulates financial business by law, 121 restricts discussion on judges, 123 is ordinances.

33.s: As per Article 274 of the Indian Constitution, the prior recommendation of the ___ is required to Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested.
33.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
33.x: Art. 274 requires the President's prior recommendation for Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested.

33.s:
Prior sanction of the President of India is required before introducing a Bill in the Parliament on –
1. Formation of a new State
2. Affecting taxation in which States are interested
3. Altering the boundaries of the States
4. Money bill Considering the above statements, select the correct answer from the code given below:
33.x: All four need the President's prior recommendation: new States and boundary changes (Art. 3), taxation in which States are interested (Art. 274) and Money Bills (Arts. 109, 117).

33.s: Which bill can be introduced without the prior recommendation of the President of India?
33.x: An ordinary Bill needs no prior recommendation of the President (except listed cases); Money Bills and Financial Bills (the Finance Bill is usually a Money Bill) need it.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
33.x: Article 113 deals with Demands for Grants; the Appropriation Bill is under Article 114.
n: Articles 109 and 110 deal with Money Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Articles 112 to 114 deal with the Budget, Demands for Grants, and the Appropriation Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Article 117 deals with Financial Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Article 368 deals with constitutional amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: **Article 108:** **Joint Sittings**; **Article 111:** **Presidential Assent**.
**Article 116:** **Vote-on-Account**.
**Articles 200 and 201:** assent to **State Bills**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Money Bill — Joint sitting not permitted
33.x: A Financial Bill-I does not require the Speaker's certificate. A Money Bill requires that certificate; joint sitting is permitted for Financial Bills-I and II but not for a Money Bill.
33.tq: Check the certification column separately from the House of introduction and joint-sitting columns.
xs: **Financial Bill-I — Speaker's certificate required** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct; FB-I needs **no** certificate.
The rest are right: a Money Bill needs the certificate and has **no joint sitting**; FB-II allows a joint sitting.
xa: FB-I: **only LS**, minister only, President's recommendation **at introduction**.
The President **can return** FB-I and FB-II but not a Money Bill.
Every money bill is a financial bill, but **not every financial bill** a money bill.

33.s: In which House can a Financial Bill-I under Article 117(1) be introduced?
33.x: It is introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject it.
xa: FB-I contains Art. 110 matters **partially, plus other matters**; no Speaker's certificate.
A **joint sitting** is allowed for FB-I.
Amendments **reducing/abolishing** a tax need no recommendation; those **increasing** a tax do.

33.s: Which Bill gives effect to the tax proposals of the Budget?
33.x: The Finance Bill gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals; every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.
xa: The Finance Bill is **usually certified a Money Bill**.
⚠ Trap: some notes reverse the definitions.

33.s: A Financial Bill-II under Article 117(3) needs the President's recommendation at which stage?
33.x: A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House and needs the President's recommendation only at the consideration stage.

33.s: A proposed amendment to a Financial Bill-I seeks to abolish an existing tax. Is the President's recommendation required for such an amendment?
o: No, because Financial Bills-I never require recommendation
Yes, because every amendment to a tax requires recommendation
No, an amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require such recommendation
Yes, but only when the Bill is pending in the Rajya Sabha
33.x: An amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require the President's recommendation. An amendment increasing a tax requires such recommendation.
33.tq: Distinguish the direction of the tax change; reducing or abolishing tax is treated differently from increasing it.
xs: No — an amendment **reducing or abolishing** a tax needs **no** President's recommendation — so option **(3)** is correct.
An amendment **increasing** a tax **does** need it — so option (1) "never" and option (2) "every amendment" are wrong.
xa: FB-I itself needs the President's recommendation **at introduction** and starts **only in LS**.
The RS can **amend or reject** FB-I.
FB-I can go to a **joint sitting**.

33.s: Which of the following Bills may be introduced by a private member?
33.x: Only a Financial Bill-II may be introduced by a minister or a private member; Money Bills (including the Appropriation Bill) and FB-I by a minister only.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
33.x: Financial Bill-I is under Article 117(1); the Money Bill is defined in Article 110, FB-II is Article 117(3) and the joint sitting is Article 108.

33.s: Which of the following is NOT required for a Financial Bill-I?
o: Introduction only in the Lok Sabha
33.x: A Financial Bill-I needs no Speaker's certificate; that is required only for a Money Bill.

33.s: Which Bill, giving effect to the tax proposals of the Budget, is usually certified by the Speaker as a Money Bill?
33.x: The Finance Bill puts the Budget's tax proposals into effect and is usually certified as a Money Bill.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 117(3) — Financial Bill-II at the consideration stage
Article 3 — Formation of new States or alteration of their areas, boundaries or names
Article 274 — Bills relating exclusively to expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India
33.x: Article 274 concerns Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested. Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India require recommendation under Article 117(3).
33.tq: Use the Article-subject match and reject the swapped Article 274 description.
xs: **Article 274 — expenditure from the CFI** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 274** covers bills affecting **taxation in which states are interested**; CFI expenditure bills fall under **Art. 117(3)**.
The others are right: **Art. 3** = new states/boundaries/names; **Art. 117(1)** = FB-I.
xa: Art. 3 bills need the President's prior recommendation and may start in **either House**.
**Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026** (to "Keralam") was under **Art. 3**.
Money Bills and **FB-I** cannot originate in the Rajya Sabha.

33.s: What does a State Bill imposing restrictions on inter-state trade need before its introduction in the State Legislature?
33.x: A State Bill restricting inter-state trade needs the President's previous sanction before introduction.

33.s: Under which Article does a Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested need the President's prior recommendation?
33.x: Article 274 requires the President's prior recommendation for Bills on taxation in which States are interested.

33.x: Every Bill passes through three readings in each House – first reading (introduction), second reading (discussion, committee and clause-by-clause stage) and third reading (passing).

33.s: All legislative proposals are brought before the Parliament in the form of:
33.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
33.x: Every legislative proposal comes before Parliament as a Bill, which becomes an Act after passage and the President's assent.

33.s: The President of India has no authority
o: to summon a joint sitting of Parliament
to return advice given by the Union Cabinet
33.x: The President can summon a joint sitting, prorogue the Houses and return Cabinet advice once (Art. 74(1)); he dissolves only the Lok Sabha – the Rajya Sabha is permanent, so he cannot dissolve 'Parliament'.

33.s: Which of the following Bills was discussed in the Lok Sabha but was withdrawn before it could be discussed in the Rajya Sabha?
33.x: The Defamation Bill, 1988 was passed by the Lok Sabha but withdrawn by the government after press protests before it was taken up in the Rajya Sabha.

33.s: A Bill presented in Parliament becomes an Act after –
o: It is passed by both the Houses
The President has given his Assent
The Prime Minister has signed it
The Supreme Court has declared it to be within the
33.x: A Bill passed by both Houses becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Art. 111).

33.s: A legislative bill may be introduced in which House of Parliament?
33.x: An ordinary (legislative) Bill may be introduced in either House; only Money Bills and Financial Bills I must begin in the Lok Sabha.

33.s: A private member bill to regulate the appointment of judges through the National Judicial Commission was introduced in Rajya Sabha by ... in December 2022.
33.src: APPSC Group-IV Paper-I (Mains) General Studies & Mental Abil
33.x: On 9 Dec 2022 CPI(M) MP Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharyya introduced the private member's National Judicial Commission Bill, 2022 in the Rajya Sabha.

33.s:
In the context of distinctions existing between a Public Bill and a Private Bill, select the statement/statements that is/are valid:

I. A Private Bill which has been introduced by a Member of Parliament sitting in the opposition and which has been approved by the House will have to be referred to the law department for consultation.

II. A Public Bill is always introduced in the Parliament by the Minister or a member of the government party.

III. A Private Bill will not reflect the policy of the government but upon its approval by the House, a Private Bill would have reflected the policy of the government.

IV. Public Bills and Private Bills, regardless of the differences between them, are governed by the same general procedure, and are required to be passed through the same stages in the House.
33.x: Only IV: both Bills follow the same procedure and stages. I is wrong (a private Bill is drafted by the member, not referred to the law department); II is wrong (a public Bill is introduced only by a minister); III is wrong (a private Bill does not become government policy).

33.s: The Government Bill means a Bill introduced by a
o: Member of the Treasury bench in the Lok Sabha.
Member of the Parliament who is not a Minister.
Minister in any House of the Parliament.
33.x: A Government Bill is introduced by a minister, who can belong to either House; a non-minister's Bill is a private member's Bill.

33.s:
With reference to the Parliament of India, consider the following statements.

I. A private member’s bill is a bill presented by a Member of Parliament who is not elected but only nominated by the President of India.

II. Recently, a private member’s bill has been passed in the Parliament of India for the first time in its history.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
33.x: I is wrong – any non-minister MP, not only a nominated one, moves a private member's Bill; II is wrong – 14 such Bills have become law, the last in 1970. So neither.

33.s: How many readings would a bill undergo in a house of Parliament before it is passed?
33.src: APPSC Teaching Staff of the Department of Technical Educatio
33.x: A Bill undergoes three readings in each House before it is passed.

33.s: During which of the following stages, division of vote would be taken on a Bill introduced in Lok Sabha?
33.x: At the third reading the Bill as a whole is put to the vote and accepted or rejected – that is the formal division on the Bill.

33.s: At which of the following stages general discussion on a Bill takes place in the Lok Sabha?
33.x: General discussion on the principles of a Bill takes place at the second reading; the first reading is introduction and the third is passing.

33.s: The creation of a new All-India Service under Article 312 begins with a resolution of which body?
33.x: Creation of a new All-India Service starts with a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312.

33.s: A Government Bill in Parliament ordinarily requires what period of notice before introduction, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires what period?
33.x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.
33.tq: Compare the two notice periods directly and watch for their reversal in the options.
xs: A Government Bill needs **7 days'** notice and a Private Member's Bill **1 month's** notice — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the two; **14 days** is the Rajya Sabha's limit for returning a Money Bill, not a notice period.
xa: A Government Bill is introduced by a **minister**; a Private Member's Bill by any MP who is **not a minister**.
Rejection of a Government Bill signals **loss of confidence**; defeat of a private bill does not affect the government.
Only **14** private members' bills have become law, the last in **1970**.

33.s: Who normally drafts a Government Bill?
o: Concerned department in association with the Law Ministry
33.x: A Government Bill is drafted by the concerned department with the Law Ministry; a Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member.
xa: Notice: Government Bill **7 days**; Private Member's Bill **1 month**.
The LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** classifies them and allots time.
Defeat of a Private Member's Bill has **no bearing** on the government.

33.s: In which year was the last Private Member's Bill enacted into law?
33.x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in 1970.
xa: A Private Member's Bill is introduced by any MP who is **not a minister**, with **1 month's** notice.
Its defeat does **not affect** the government.
The LS **Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** classifies them and allots time.

33.s: In the Rajya Sabha, which committee allots time for Private Members' Bills?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
33.x: The Rajya Sabha has no Committee on Private Members' Bills; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.
xa: A **private member's bill** needs **1 month's** notice; a **government bill** **7 days'**.
Only **14** private members' bills have become law, the last in **1970**.
Defeat of a private member's bill has **no bearing** on the government.

33.s: In the Lok Sabha, which committee allots time for Private Members' Bills?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
33.x: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions allots the time; defeat of such a Bill has no bearing on the government.
xa: In the **Rajya Sabha**, the **Business Advisory Committee** allots time.
Notice for a Private Member's Bill: **1 month**.
Only **14** have become law, the last in **1970**.

33.s: How many Private Members' Bills have become law so far?
33.x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in 1970.

33.s: Who can introduce a Private Member's Bill?
o: Any MP who is not a minister
Only the Leader of the Opposition
33.x: Any MP who is not a minister may introduce a Private Member's Bill; Government Bills are introduced by ministers.

33.s: What does the defeat of a Government Bill in the House signal?
o: Automatic dissolution of the Lok Sabha
Reference of the Bill to a joint sitting
Loss of confidence in the government
33.x: Defeat of a Government Bill signals loss of confidence; defeat of a Private Member's Bill has no bearing on the government.

33.s: Which of the following is correct about Government Bills and Private Members' Bills?
o: A Private Member's Bill is passed in a single reading
A Government Bill needs one month's notice for introduction
A Private Member's Bill is drafted by the Law Ministry
Both pass through the same readings and stages in each House
33.x: Government and Private Members' Bills follow the same general procedure and stages. A Government Bill needs 7 days' notice and is drafted by the department with the Law Ministry.

33.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Private Member's Bill needs one month's notice before introduction.
2. The defeat of a Private Member's Bill means loss of confidence in the government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
33.x: A Private Member's Bill needs one month's notice. Its defeat has no bearing on the government; only the defeat of a Government Bill signals loss of confidence.

33.s: Which committee of the Lok Sabha examines Private Members' Bills seeking to amend the Constitution before they are introduced?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
33.x: In the Lok Sabha, the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions classifies such Bills, allots time and examines private members' constitutional amendment Bills before introduction.

33.s: At which stage of a Bill does clause-by-clause consideration take place?
33.x: The Second Reading covers general discussion, committee stage and clause-by-clause voting; the Third Reading concerns the Bill as a whole.
xa: Three readings take place in **each House** (APPSC-GS 2018).
At the third reading **no amendments of substance** are allowed.
The second House may pass, amend, reject, or keep the bill for **6 months**.

33.s: After an ordinary Bill is passed by one House, what may the other House do?
o: Return it only to the President
Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
33.x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
33.tq: Choose the option that lists the complete range of legislative responses rather than an exclusive power.
xs: The second House may **pass, amend, reject, or keep it pending for six months** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only the **Speaker certifies** Money Bills, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: A deadlock leads to a **joint sitting** (**Art. 108**).
Joint sitting ground: not passed for **more than six months**, excluding prorogation/adjournment over **4 consecutive days**.
An ordinary bill may be introduced in **either House**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
33.x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
33.tq: Separate the four veto types by their effect and by whether the Indian President possesses them.
xs: **Suspensive veto** — the President may **return a non-money bill**, but **must assent** if it is re-passed — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) is wrong: **no time limit** is fixed, which is why a **pocket veto** is possible.
xa: Art. 111 options: **give assent, withhold assent, return for reconsideration**.
Re-passage may be **with or without amendment**.
A **Money Bill** cannot be returned by the President.

33.s: Which Amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill?
33.x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made it obligatory for the President to assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the second House on an ordinary Bill:
1. It may keep the Bill pending for six months, leading to a deadlock.
2. It must return the Bill within 14 days.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
33.x: For an ordinary Bill the second House has no time limit; the 14-day limit applies to the Rajya Sabha on a Money Bill.

33.s: A Bill is published in the Gazette at which stage of its passage?
33.x: At the first reading the Bill is introduced, its title and objectives are read and it is published in the Gazette.

33.s: If a Bill returned by the President is passed again by Parliament, the President must assent. What is this power called?
33.x: Returning a Bill once is a suspensive veto; if re-passed, with or without amendment, the President must assent.

33.s: Why is a 'pocket veto' possible for the President of India?
o: The President can return a Bill any number of times
The Constitution fixes no time limit for the President to decide on a Bill
The President can reject a Money Bill after the Rajya Sabha passes it
The President can refer every Bill to a joint sitting
33.x: Article 111 sets no time limit for the President's decision, so the President can keep a Bill pending. India has no qualified veto.

33.s: Which of the following Bills can the President NOT return to Parliament for reconsideration?
33.x: A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration, whereas Financial Bills-I and II can be.

33.s: What happens to pending bills when a Parliamentary session is adjourned sine die?
o: They lapse and cannot be taken up in the next session
They are sent back to the lower house for reconsideration
They are automatically passed into law
They continue to remain active and can be taken up in the next session
33.src: APPSC AEE (Civil), AMVI, Agriculture Officer and Other Posts
33.x: Adjournment sine die does not affect pending Bills; they remain alive and are taken up in the next session.

33.s:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

A. A bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its prorogation.

B. A bill pending in the Rajya Sabha, which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha, shall not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
33.x: A is wrong – prorogation does not make a Bill lapse; B is right – a Bill pending in the RS not passed by the LS survives dissolution.

33.s:
In connection with the lapsing of Bills, which of the following statement/statements is/are valid?

I. If the Lok Sabha has passed the Bill, but if the Bill has still not been discussed in the Rajya Sabha, then such a Bill does not lapse.

36.s: Regarding the provisions related to disqualification on grounds of defection, choose the wrong answer
o: A member of the house belonging to any political party has voluntarily given up his membership of such party would be disqualified
Votes or abstain from voting in such house contrary to any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs would lead to disqualification
A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a member of the house if he joins any political party after the expiration of six months from the date on which he takes his seat
If a party expel a legislator from the party, expelled member loses his seat in the house
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: An expelled member does not lose his seat: he continues to belong to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes (G. Viswanathan 1996) and sits as unattached. Giving up membership, defying the whip and a nominated member joining a party after six months are grounds of disqualification.

36.s: Regarding anti defection, which of the following is not correct?
o: If a member defects from one party to some other party he is disqualified by the speaker
If a party expels an elected member of the party, the Member does not lose his seat in Legislature immediately
If a group of one-Third of members of the party decided to split, they will not lose their seats
If a group of 2/3 of the total members of a party decide to merge with some other party
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: Since the 91st Amendment (2003) a one-third split no longer protects members, so that statement is not correct. A defector is disqualified by the Speaker, an expelled member keeps his seat, and a two-thirds merger is protected.

36.s: Which one of the following is a major criticism of the anti-defection law mentioned in the context of Indian parliamentary practice?
o: It stifles intra-party dissent and legislators’ free expression without necessarily stopping mass defections.
It has abolished the Speaker’s authority over the House.
It prevents all coalition governments from being formed.
It applies exclusively to nominated Members of Parliament.
36.x: Critics argue that the law suppresses intra-party dissent and free expression, while failing to prevent mass defections effectively. The other statements do not describe the criticism.
36.tq: Find the option that captures both sides of the criticism rather than an absolute consequence.
xs: The law **stifles intra-party dissent and free expression** without stopping **mass defections** — option **(1)**.
The Speaker still decides disqualification (**Para 6**); the law covers party, independent and nominated members, not only nominated.
xa: Critics say the law has been left "**impotent**".
**Speaker not neutral**: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.

36.s:
Assertion (A): An MP or MLA may be treated as having voluntarily given up party membership even without formally resigning.
Reason (R): Conduct such as publicly campaigning for an opposition party can constitute voluntarily giving up membership.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
36.x: Both are true: a member can be held to have given up party membership without resigning, because conduct such as campaigning for a rival party counts. R explains A.
36.tq: Recall that conduct can amount to giving up membership.
n: Voluntarily giving up party membership is broader than formal resignation and includes conduct. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An MP or MLA can be considered to have voluntarily given up party membership by publicly campaigning for an opposition party. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An MP or MLA can be considered to have voluntarily given up party membership without submitting a formal resignation letter. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
"**Voluntarily giving up membership**" is **broader** than **formal resignation** — it can be inferred from **conduct**.
**Publicly campaigning** for an **opposition party**, even without a resignation letter, counts — which explains A.
xa: **Ravi S. Naik v UoI (1994)**: voluntarily giving up membership is **not the same as resigning**.
**G. Viswanathan (1996)**: an **expelled** member **still belongs** to his party; joining another party = giving up membership.
Other ground: **voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip** without **prior permission** (**Para 2(1)(b)**).

36.s: Under the Tenth Schedule, a nominated member is disqualified if he joins a political party after how much time?
36.x: A nominated member may join a party within six months of taking his seat; joining after six months disqualifies him.
n: A party-elected member is disqualified for voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip without prior permission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An independent elected member is disqualified for joining any political party after election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A nominated member is disqualified for joining a political party after the expiry of six months from taking a seat. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party while holding office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party after vacating office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]

36.s: Which of the following does NOT protect a member from disqualification under the present anti-defection law?
o: Prior permission of the party for the vote
The party condoning the vote within 15 days
A split by one-third of the legislature party
A merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party
36.x: The one-third split exception was deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003); prior permission, condonation within 15 days and a two-thirds merger still protect a member.
n: A party-elected member is protected from disqualification when prior permission is obtained. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A party-elected member is protected from disqualification when the party condones the action within 15 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A merger is an exception when at least two-thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge with another party. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]

36.s: Under the Tenth Schedule, on which ground is an independent elected member disqualified?
o: Becomes a Minister without joining a party
Joins any political party after election
Supports the ruling side on a confidence motion
Abstains on a vote in the House
36.x: An independent member is disqualified only on joining a party after election; becoming a Minister without joining a party does not disqualify him.
n: An independent elected member is disqualified for joining any political party after election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An independent elected member is disqualified for joining the government as an independent minister without taking party membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]

36.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding a Presiding Officer under the Anti-Defection Law?
o: A Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party after vacating office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party while holding office.
A Presiding Officer can voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair.
36.x: Option A is incorrect: a presiding officer may give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin the party after leaving office. Joining another party, during or after the term, disqualifies them.
36.tq: Discriminate rejoining the original party from joining another.
n: A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party while holding office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party after vacating office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may rejoin the original party after demitting office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
A Presiding Officer **may voluntarily give up** party membership on **election to the Chair** and **rejoin** the original party after demitting office.
He is disqualified only for **joining another political party** while holding office or after vacating it — so options (2), (3), (4) are true.
xa: This exception is **Para 5**, covering **Speaker/Deputy Speaker/Chairman/Deputy Chairman**; it is **in force**.
Criticism: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**, so they are seen as partisan.
The Presiding Officer decides defection petitions under **Para 6**.

36.s: Voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip without prior permission is a ground of disqualification under which paragraph of the Tenth Schedule?
36.x: Defying the whip is covered by Para 2(1)(b); Para 4 is the merger exception, Para 5 concerns presiding officers and Para 6 the deciding authority.

36.s: Under Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule, on which ground is a Presiding Officer disqualified?
o: Leaves his party on election to the office
Rejoins his party after vacating office
Remains a member of his party while in office
36.x: Para 5 lets a Presiding Officer leave his party on election and rejoin after office; joining another party disqualifies him.

36.s: Within how many days may a political party condone a member's vote against its whip, so that the member is not disqualified?
36.x: Under the Tenth Schedule, a member who votes or abstains against the whip is not disqualified if the party condones it within 15 days.

36.s: Why has the two-thirds rule under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule been criticised?
o: Protect individual dissent against the whip
36.x: The Paragraph 4 two-thirds rule has been used as a defence for mass defection and so attracts criticism.
xa: **AAP**: **7 of 10** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a "merger" with the BJP (Apr **2026**).
**TMC**: **20** Lok Sabha MPs told Speaker **Om Birla** they would merge with the **NPCI**.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators **cannot by themselves** create a "deemed merger".
**Law Commission's 170th Report (1999)** wanted the **split and merger exceptions deleted**.

36.s: Under Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule, what is required for protection from disqualification on the ground of merger?
o: two-thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge and the original political party also merges
all members of the legislature party join another party
one-half of the legislature party joins another party
the Speaker alone approves the merger
36.x: A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.
36.tq: Apply both cumulative tests for a valid merger instead of relying only on the numerical threshold.
xs: A valid merger needs **two-thirds of the legislature party** to agree **and** the **original political party** to merge — option **(1)**.
These are the **two tests** in **Para 4**.
Two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a "**deemed merger**" (**Subhash Desai**, 2023).
xa: Neither those who merge nor those who stay are disqualified.
⚠ **Merger = two-thirds** (Para 4, in force); **Split = one-third** (Para 3, deleted **2003**).
**June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP Rajya Sabha MPs** "merged" with BJP under Para 4.
Misuse: Para 4 used as a **defence for mass defection** (AAP, TMC cases, **2026**).

36.s: Regarding the privileges of the parliament, choose the wrong answer?
o: Constitution guaranteed freedom of speech in parliament
The Members of parliament are immune from arrest in Civil cases whether the parliament is in session or not.
In Criminal cases parliament members cannot be arrested while they are in the House in Session
Parliament has freedom to publish its proceedings
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: Freedom from arrest applies only in civil cases and only during a session and 40 days before and after it, not 'whether Parliament is in session or not'. Free speech (Art. 105(1)), the right to publish proceedings and the rule that no member is arrested within the precincts without the presiding officer's permission are all correct.

36.s: Which of the following punishments can be awarded by the Lok Sabha to a member held guilty of breach of privileges or contempt of the House?
o: Expulsion from the House and thereby declaring his seat as vacant
36.x: A House punishes members and outsiders by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion (Raja Ram Pal 2007 upheld expulsion). It does not impose fines, and imprisonment lasts only till the session ends, so 'six months' is wrong.

36.s: Which of the following punishments can the Lok Sabha impose on members who behave in breach of privilege or contempt of the House?
o: Expelling from the House and declaring the seat vacant
36.x: A House punishes by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion. It does not impose fines, and imprisonment cannot outlast the session, so expulsion with the seat declared vacant is the valid option.

36.s: Which of the following statement is correct regarding Parliamentary Privileges?
o: Parliamentary Privileges are the privileges tha are enjoyed collectively by each House of the Parliament, and not by the Members individually
Only Members can be punished for contempt by reprimand and admonition but not outsiders
The phrase 'Breach of Privilege' has wider implications than the 'Contempt of the House
The Members cannot be arrested during the session of Parliament but this privilege is available only in civil cases and not in criminal cases or preventive detention cases
36.x: Members cannot be arrested during a session and 40 days before and after it, but only in civil cases, not criminal or preventive detention cases. Privileges are both collective and individual, outsiders can be punished too, and contempt is wider than breach of privilege.

36.s: All following statements regarding the privileges of Parliament members are correct except
36.x: Members' individual privileges include freedom of speech, freedom from arrest in civil cases and freedom from attendance as a witness while the House sits. Privileges are also collective (of each House), so 'only individual freedom' is the incorrect statement.

36.s: Under which Article of the Constitution the Courts have been prohibited from inquiring the proceedings of the Parliament?
36.x: Article 122 bars courts from inquiring into the validity of proceedings of Parliament on the ground of irregularity of procedure (Art. 212 for States).

36.s: The powers, privileges and immunities of either House of Parliament and of its Committee and Members have mainly be laid down in Article ……… of the Constitution of India.
36.x: Article 105 (Art. 194 for State Legislatures) lays down the powers, privileges and immunities of each House of Parliament, its members and committees.

36.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary privileges?
o: Article 105 protects freedom of speech in Parliament
Article 194 protects freedom of speech in State Legislatures
Privileges are fully codified in a single parliamentary statute
Privileges also rest on conventions, rules, statutes and judicial rulings
36.x: Parliamentary privileges have never been codified in a single statute; they rest on conventions, rules, statutes and court rulings. Articles 105 and 194 give the speech protection.

36.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 105 – Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
36.x: Article 194 deals with State Legislature privileges; Article 105 with Parliament's privileges, Article 122 with parliamentary proceedings and Article 212 with State Legislature proceedings.
xa: Pairing trick: Parliament articles **105/122**, state articles **194/212**.
Privilege notices: **LS Rule 222** / **RS Rule 187**, usually after **Question Hour**.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.

36.s: In Raja Ram Pal (2007), what did the Supreme Court hold about decisions of a House in matters of privilege?
o: Reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality
Reviewable on every ground of procedural irregularity
Subject to approval by the President
36.x: Raja Ram Pal (2007) held that privilege decisions can be reviewed, but only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality. They are not wholly immune; mere procedural irregularity is protected by Art. 122/212; the President has no approving role.
36.tq: Raja Ram Pal 2007 = limited review of privilege decisions.
xs: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions are **reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality** — option **(2)**.
So they are not wholly immune (option 1 wrong).
Mere **procedural irregularity** is shielded by **Art. 122/212**, so option (3) is wrong; the President has no approving role.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024)**: **7-judge Bench**, **no immunity for bribery** to speak or vote.
Final say on a privilege notice lies with the **House**, after the **Privileges Committee** recommends.
Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.

36.s: Under which rules does a Member of Parliament generally raise a breach of privilege or contempt by a minister, another member or an outsider?
o: Lok Sabha Rule 187 or Rajya Sabha Rule 222
Lok Sabha Rule 222 or Rajya Sabha Rule 187
36.x: Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.
36.tq: Test the paired procedural rules while guarding against a deliberate reversal of the two Houses.
xs: A privilege notice is raised under **Lok Sabha Rule 222 / Rajya Sabha Rule 187** — option **(3)**.
It is usually raised **after Question Hour**; any MP can allege breach by a **minister, member or outsider**.
Option (1) swaps the rules; **Arts 103/192** deal with other disqualifications; **Para 6** of the Tenth Schedule is about defection.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS**.
Presiding Officer grants/denies consent → House decides or refers to **Privileges Committee**.
**RS Privileges Committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.

36.s: In a breach of privilege case, who takes the final decision on action against the offender?
36.x: The Committee of Privileges examines and recommends, but the House takes the final decision.
xa: Notice is raised under **LS Rule 222 / RS Rule 187**, usually after **Question Hour**.
**RS committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.
**Contempt** is wider than breach: any act **obstructing the House** or its members.

36.s: Which of the following best distinguishes contempt of the House from breach of privilege?
o: Contempt is wider and includes any act obstructing the House or its members in their functions
Contempt is narrower and concerns only members of the House
Breach of privilege applies only to ministers, whereas contempt applies only to outsiders
There is no distinction between the two expressions
36.x: Contempt has a wider scope and includes acts that obstruct the House or its members in the discharge of their functions. A breach concerns infringement of a specific privilege.
36.tq: Discriminate between the broader concept and the specific infringement instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: **Contempt is wider** — any act **obstructing the House or its members in their functions** — option **(1)**.
So contempt is not narrower (option 2), and the two terms are distinct (option 4 wrong).
A privilege notice can allege breach or contempt by a **minister, member or outsider**, so option (3)'s split is wrong.
xa: Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.
**Maharashtra**: the **Legislative Council's Privileges Committee** summoned **Kunal Kamra** on a breach notice.
Privileges rest on **conventions**, rules, statutes and judicial rulings — **never codified**.

36.s: What is the composition of the Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha?
o: 10 members usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman
22 members chaired by the Leader of the Opposition
31 members chaired by a member of the ruling party
36.x: The Rajya Sabha Privileges Committee has 10 members and is usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman. Fifteen members is the Lok Sabha committee's strength; 22 and 31 are PAC/COPU and DRSC sizes.
xs: The **Rajya Sabha** Privileges Committee has **10 members**, **usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman** — option **(2)**.
It examines witnesses and **recommends**; the **House decides**.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS** for privilege notices.
The Presiding Officer may let the House decide or refer the matter to the **Privileges Committee**.
**Maharashtra Legislative Council's** committee summoned **Kunal Kamra**.

36.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 75(1A) — Fifteen per cent limit on the Union Council of Ministers
Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule — Split exception
Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule — Merger exception
Article 105(1)-(2) — Fifteen per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers
36.x: Article 105(1)-(2) concerns freedom of speech and related parliamentary privileges. The 15 per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers is provided under Article 164(1A).
36.tq: Find the wrong authority-provision pairing by separating privilege provisions from ministerial-limit provisions.
xs: **Article 105(1)-(2)** is wrongly paired: it is about **freedom of speech / privileges** — option **(4)**.
The **15%** cap on a **State** Council of Ministers is **Art. 164(1A)**.
The other pairs are correct: **Art. 75(1A)** = Union **15%** cap; **Para 3** = split; **Para 4** = merger.
xa: **Art. 164(1A)** sets a minimum of **12** ministers.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B** bar a disqualified defector from ministerial/remunerative posts.
All came via the **91st Amendment, 2003**.

36.s: What did the Supreme Court hold about legislative privilege in Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)?
o: gives no immunity for bribery connected with speaking or voting
gives complete immunity for accepting a bribe to speak or vote
applies only to proceedings of State Legislatures
overrides the power of courts to investigate corruption
36.x: The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
36.tq: Use the later larger-Bench decision to identify the overruling of an earlier precedent.
xs: **Sita Soren (2024)** held privilege **gives no immunity for bribery** connected with speaking or voting — option **(1)**.
A **7-judge Bench** gave the ruling and **overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**, which had allowed such immunity.
So option (2) states the overruled position; the ruling is not limited to State Legislatures.
xa: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.
Privilege source: **Art. 105** (Parliament) and **Art. 194** (states).
⚠ **P.V. Narasimha Rao** = **1998** (overruled); **Sita Soren** = **2024**.

36.s: Which Article bars courts from questioning proceedings of Parliament on the ground of procedural irregularity?
36.x: Article 122 protects proceedings of Parliament from court inquiry for procedural irregularity; Article 212 does the same for State Legislatures.

36.s: The Committee of Privileges of the Lok Sabha consists of how many members nominated by the Speaker?
36.x: The Lok Sabha Privileges Committee has 15 members nominated by the Speaker; the Rajya Sabha committee has 10.

36.s: Which earlier judgment did the seven-judge Bench of the Supreme Court overrule in Sita Soren (2024)?
36.x: Sita Soren held there is no immunity for bribery to speak or vote, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).

36.s: Which of the following punishments can a House of Parliament impose on a person found guilty of breach of privilege or contempt?
36.x: The House can punish by admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, or suspension or expulsion of a member.

36.s: Who can be punished by a House of Parliament for breach of its privileges?
36.x: Breach of privilege or contempt can be committed by members as well as outsiders, and both can be punished by the House.

36.s: In which kind of cases does the freedom from arrest of Members of Parliament apply?
o: Civil, criminal and preventive detention cases
36.x: Freedom from arrest covers only civil cases; it does not apply to criminal cases or preventive detention.

36.s: For how many days before and after a session of the House do members enjoy freedom from arrest in civil cases?
36.x: Members cannot be arrested in civil cases during a session and for 40 days before and after it.

36.s: Which of the following is a collective privilege of a House of Parliament, and not an individual privilege of its members?
o: Freedom from arrest in civil cases
Right to receive immediate information of the arrest of a member
Right to decline to give evidence in a court while the House is in session
36.x: The right to be informed at once of a member's arrest, detention or release belongs to the House; the other three are privileges of individual members.

36.s: Which of the following is NOT an individual privilege of a Member of Parliament?
o: Freedom of speech in the House
Freedom from arrest in civil cases during a session
Right to exclude strangers from the sittings of the House
36.x: Excluding strangers from its sittings is a collective privilege of the House; the others are privileges of individual members.

36.s: On any issue pertaining to the disqualification of any member of Lok Sabha under 10th Schedule of Indian Constitution, the final decision is taken by ……… .
36.x: Para 6: the Speaker decides defection disqualification of a Lok Sabha member, acting as a tribunal (subject to judicial review, Kihoto 1992). The President and the ECI have no role.

36.s:
Consider the following statements :
I. If any question arises as to whether a Member of the House of the People has become subject to disqualification under the 10th Schedule, the President's decision in accordance with the opinion of the Council of Union Ministers shall be final.
II. There is no mention of the word 'political party' in the Constitution of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: I is wrong: Tenth Schedule questions are decided by the Speaker (Lok Sabha), not the President on the Council's advice. II is wrong: the term 'political party' appears in the Tenth Schedule.

36.s: Which Article deals with disqualifications for membership of a State Legislature?
36.x: Article 191 covers State disqualifications and 190 State vacation of seats; Articles 101 and 102 are the Parliament counterparts.
n: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 amended Articles 101, 102, 190, and 191. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: The **52nd Amendment, 1985** amended all four Articles while inserting the **Tenth Schedule**.
General disqualification is decided by the **President** (**Art. 103**) or **Governor** (**Art. 192**) on the **EC's binding opinion**.

36.s: Which Articles govern defection disqualification of Members of Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively?
36.x: Defection disqualification comes under Article 102(2) for MPs and 191(2) for State legislators, read with the Tenth Schedule. Clauses (1) are the general grounds.
n: Defection disqualification is governed by the 10th Schedule and Articles 102(2) and 191(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: Defection disqualification is governed by **Articles 102(2) and 191(2)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
These Articles, read with the **10th Schedule**, cover MPs and State legislators respectively.
**Articles 102(1) and 191(1)** are the **general** disqualification grounds; **Articles 103 and 192** give the President/Governor's decision on them.
xa: **Articles 101 and 190** deal with **vacation of seats** in Parliament and State Legislatures.
General disqualifications: **President** (MP) or **Governor** (MLA/MLC), with **ECI opinion** **mandatory and binding**.
Defection matters: **Speaker or Chairman alone**, acting as a **tribunal**; subject to **judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).

36.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about general (non-defection) disqualification of legislators?
o: The President decides the question for a Union MP.
The Governor decides the question for a State MLA or MLC.
The ECI's opinion is non-binding in the case of a State legislator.
The ECI's opinion is mandatory and binding in the case of an MP.
36.x: For both MPs and State legislators the ECI's opinion is compulsory and binding.
n: The President of India must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Governor must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: ⚠ In **defection** cases the **ECI is not consulted** — the **Speaker or Chairman** decides.
The **Election Commission** and **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** proposed that defection cases too be decided by the **President or Governor on the EC's advice**.
**NCRWC (2002)**: defectors to be barred from **public or remunerative political office** for the rest of the term.

36.s: Who decides the general (non-defection) disqualification of a Member of Parliament?
o: Speaker or Chairman of the House
36.x: General disqualification of an MP is decided by the President (on the Election Commission's binding opinion); defection cases go to the Speaker or Chairman.
n: The Presiding Officer of the concerned House decides defection disqualification matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The President of India decides general disqualification matters concerning a Union MP. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Governor of the State decides general disqualification matters concerning a State MLA or MLC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer includes the Speaker or Chairman. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]

36.s: In what capacity does the Speaker or Chairman act while deciding a disqualification question under the Tenth Schedule?
36.x: The presiding officer acts as a tribunal, subject to limited judicial review; the ECI gives no opinion here (that applies under Articles 103 and 192).
xa: ⚠ Contrast: **other** disqualifications (**Arts 103 and 192**) → President/Governor decides on the **EC's opinion**.
Review grounds: **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice** or constitutional mandate.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.

36.s: Why was Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu?
o: It barred judicial review without the required ratification by the States under Article 368(2)
It transferred disqualification powers to the Election Commission
It permitted nominated members to vote in all elections
It abolished the office of the Speaker
36.x: Paragraph 7 attempted to oust the jurisdiction of courts. Its provisions were held invalid because the amendment had not been ratified by the States as required under Article 368(2).
36.tq: Match the constitutional defect with the provision that attempted to exclude court jurisdiction.
