38.x: The USA has the presidential form of government; India, Canada and Britain are parliamentary.

38.s: In a Presidential Government, all the executive powers are vested in –
38.x: In a presidential government all executive power is vested in the President, who is both head of State and head of government.

38.s: Which of the following statements are correct about Presidential system? i. President is head of the State. ii. President is head of the Government. iii. President is directly elected by the people. iv. President is accountable to legislature.
o: Only i, ii and iv are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
38.x: The US-type President is head of State and head of government and is (in effect) directly elected, but is not accountable to the legislature, so i, ii and iii.

38.s: Which of the following is correct? The main feature of a Presidential form of Government is/are –
o: The Head of the Executive is the President
The President appoints his Council of Ministers
The President cannot dissolve the Legislature
38.x: In a presidential system the President heads the executive, appoints his own secretaries (cabinet) and cannot dissolve the legislature – all three are features.

38.s: Which one of the following is a basic feature of the Presidential Government?
38.x: A single executive (the President is both head of State and of government) is the basic feature of presidential government.

38.s: In presidential form of Government, the principle is
o: President checks legislature and vice versa
38.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I 2017
38.x: Presidential government rests on separation of powers with checks and balances – the President and the legislature check each other (veto, Senate confirmation, impeachment). Fusion of powers is parliamentary; 'division of powers' describes federalism.

38.s: In which country was the Presidential form of Government first formed?
38.x: The presidential form was first formed in the USA (1787 Constitution), its oldest and purest form.

38.s: Which of the following is a feature of the presidential system?
o: A plural executive headed by a Prime Minister
Executive accountable to the legislature as in a parliamentary system
A fixed term for the executive
Fusion of executive and legislative powers
38.x: A presidential system generally has a single, directly elected executive with a fixed term, not accountable to the legislature in the parliamentary sense.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-G2 2025** key: "Accountable to the legislature" is the **wrong** feature.
The President is **both Head of State and Head of Government**.
Cabinet members **may or may not** sit in the legislature (US secretaries do not).

38.s: In a semi-presidential system, to whom is the Prime Minister responsible?
38.x: In a semi-presidential system a President and a Prime Minister coexist; the President may have real powers, while the Prime Minister is responsible to the legislature.

38.s: Which one of the following sets contains only examples of parliamentary systems?
o: United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India
United States, Brazil, India and Canada
United Kingdom, United States, Brazil and Japan
Brazil, United States, Canada and India
38.x: The United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India are examples of parliamentary systems. The United States and Brazil are presidential systems.
38.tq: Classify every country in the option before accepting an all-correct grouping.
xs: **United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India** are all parliamentary systems — option **(1)** is correct.
The **United States** (origin) and **Brazil** are **presidential** systems, which rules out options (2), (3) and (4).
xa: The parliamentary system originated in **Britain** — the **Westminster model**.
Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka** — President and PM coexist.
**France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** and **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)** have a **directly elected President** with real powers.

38.s: Which of the following countries are associated with semi-presidential systems in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist?
o: Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom and the United States
Russia, India and the United States
India, the United Kingdom and France
38.x: France, Russia and Sri Lanka are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.
38.tq: Use the complete country group and reject groups containing parliamentary or presidential examples outside the stated set.
xs: **France, Russia and Sri Lanka** are semi-presidential — option **(3)** is correct.
The **UK** and **India** are parliamentary; the **United States** is presidential — so the other options fail.
xa: **France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** + **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution):** **directly elected President** with real powers + PM responsible to the legislature.
Parliamentary: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil**, most of Latin America.
⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.

38.s: In which year was France's Fifth Republic established?
38.x: France's Fifth Republic dates from 1958.
xa: Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.
In India the President is **de jure** head; PM + Council of Ministers = **de facto** executive.
India's President is **indirectly elected** for a **5-year term**; Britain's head is a **hereditary** monarch.

38.s: In which year was Sri Lanka's semi-presidential Constitution adopted?
38.x: Sri Lanka's semi-presidential Constitution dates from 1978; France's Fifth Republic from 1958.

38.s: Which of the following countries does NOT have a semi-presidential system?
38.x: India's President is indirectly elected and nominal, so India is not semi-presidential, unlike France, Russia and Sri Lanka.

38.s: Which of the following is called the mother of Parliaments?
38.x: The British Parliament is called the 'Mother of Parliaments' (John Bright, 1865); the parliamentary form began in Britain.

38.s:
Consider the following statements:

A. The Constitution of the United States of America came into force in the year 1810.

B. All revenue bills must originate in the House of Representatives of the US Congress.

C. George W. Bush is the only President in the history of the United States of America whose father was also the President of the United States of America.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: Only B is correct: revenue bills must originate in the US House of Representatives (Art. I, s.7). A is wrong – the US Constitution came into force in 1789. C is wrong – John Quincy Adams, son of John Adams, was also a President's son.

38.s: Which of the following would not be a feature of the Indian Constitution ?
o: A written, lengthy and comprehensive document
A document that has been framed after ransacking all the known Constitutions of the world
Parliamentary System at the Centre and the States
38.src: AP Grama Ward Sachivalayam Village Horticulture Assistant 20
38.x: Sovereignty of Parliament is a British feature; India has constitutional supremacy with judicial review. The other three are features of the Indian Constitution.

38.s: The Indian parliamentary system is different from the British parliamentary system in that India has
o: both a real and a nominal executive
38.x: India, unlike Britain, has judicial review – courts can strike down laws. A real and nominal executive, collective responsibility and bicameralism exist in both.

38.s:
Of the following political features, which is/are common to Indian and the USA?

I. Residuary powers vested in the centre.

II. Residuary powers vested in the states.

III. President has the power of pocket veto.

IV. The upper house has some nominated members.
Codes
38.x: Only the pocket veto is common: both the Indian and US Presidents have it. Residuary powers lie with the Union in India but with the States in the USA, and only India's upper house has nominated members.

38.s: Which of the following features is associated with Britain but not with India in the same form?
o: Collective responsibility to the lower House
38.x: Britain has an institutionalised shadow cabinet, legal ministerial responsibility and ministers who must be MPs; India lacks these in the same form.
xa: Common to both: the PM's role is so large it is called **"Prime Ministerial Government"**.
Britain: **hereditary** monarch, **unitary** state, **sovereignty of Parliament**.
India: **indirectly elected** President, **federal** state, **constitutional supremacy**.

38.s: In India, to what is the removal of the Prime Minister's government linked?
o: A decision of the ruling party
38.x: In India, removal is linked to losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha, whereas in the UK the ruling party can replace its Prime Minister.

38.s: In which country did the Westminster model of parliamentary government originate?
38.x: The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is commonly called the Westminster model.
38.tq: Recall the origin country without confusing it with countries that later adopted the system.
xs: The **Westminster model** of parliamentary government originated in **Britain** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **USA** is the origin of the **presidential** system, so option (2) is wrong.
**India** and **Japan** follow the parliamentary model but did not originate it.
xa: ⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.
Parliamentary examples: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil** and most of **Latin America**.
Semi-presidential: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.

38.s: In Britain, from which House is the Prime Minister drawn?
38.x: The British Prime Minister is drawn from the House of Commons; in India the Prime Minister may belong to either House.

38.s: Which of the following applies to the Indian Parliament but not to the British Parliament?
o: Hereditary monarch as head of state
Subject to the basic structure doctrine
38.x: The basic structure doctrine belongs to the Indian constitutional framework; sovereignty of Parliament, a hereditary monarch and the shadow cabinet are British.

38.s: The British system rests on sovereignty of Parliament. On what does the Indian system rest?
38.x: India has a written Constitution and constitutional supremacy; Britain has sovereignty of Parliament.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian and British systems:
1. India's Head of State is indirectly elected for five years.
2. British courts can strike down Acts of Parliament.
3. Britain's Constitution is unwritten.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: India's President is indirectly elected for five years and Britain's Constitution is unwritten; British courts cannot question Acts of Parliament.

38.s: In India, from which House of Parliament can the Prime Minister be drawn?
38.x: In India the Prime Minister may be a member of either House, whereas in Britain the Prime Minister comes from the House of Commons.

38.s: Which of the following features is found in the British system but not in the Indian system?
o: Collective responsibility to the lower House
Prime Minister as leader of the majority party
38.x: In Britain ministers are legally responsible (a minister must countersign acts of the Crown); India has no such legal responsibility of ministers.

38.s: On what is judicial review based in India and in the USA, respectively?
o: Due process of law; procedure established by law
Procedure established by law; due process of law
Due process of law in both
Procedure established by law in both
38.x: India follows the narrower 'procedure established by law', while the USA follows the wider 'due process of law' standard.
xa: Because of its wide review, the US Supreme Court is called a **"third chamber"**.
Both countries have an **independent judiciary with judicial review**.
Britain: courts **cannot question Acts of Parliament**.

38.s: In which year did the United States adopt the 22nd Amendment, associated with limiting presidential tenure?
38.x: The US adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951; India has no term limit for its Prime Minister.
xa: He passed **Pawan Kumar Chamling** (**8,930** days).
A **fixed term** is a feature of the **presidential** executive.
**Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.

38.s: In the USA, in whom are the residuary powers of legislation vested?
38.x: Residuary powers lie with the States in the USA and with Parliament (the Union) in India.

38.s: Which of the following is NOT common to India and the USA?
o: Residuary powers vested in the States
38.x: Residuary powers lie with the States only in the USA; in India they lie with the Union. The other three are common.

38.s: On 22 March 2026, Narendra Modi passed whose record as the longest-serving head of an elected government?
38.x: Modi completed 8,931 days, passing Pawan Kumar Chamling's 8,930; India has no term limit for the PM, unlike the US 22nd Amendment.

38.s: Because of its wide power of judicial review, which country's Supreme Court has been called a 'third chamber' of the legislature?
38.x: The US Supreme Court uses 'due process of law' and has wide judicial review, so it is called a 'third chamber'.

38.s: The main advantage of the parliamentary form of government is that
o: the executive and legislature work independently.
it provides continuity of policy and is more efficient.
the executive remains responsible to the legislature.
the head of the government cannot be changed without election.
38.x: The main advantage is that the executive stays responsible to the legislature (responsible government); continuity of policy is a presidential advantage and parliamentary governments can change without election.

38.s: The main advantage of the parliamentary form of government is that
o: the executive and legislature work independently
it provides continuity of policy and is more efficient
the executive remains responsible to the legislature
the head of the government cannot be changed without
38.x: The main advantage of the parliamentary form is that the executive remains responsible to the legislature (UPSC 2017 key).

38.s: Who said, “Parliamentary system provides a daily as well as a periodic assessment of the Government”?
38.x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly (4 Nov 1948) that the parliamentary system gives a daily assessment of responsibility (questions, motions, debates) as well as a periodic one by the electorate, which he found more effective than the American periodic assessment.

38.s:
Two statements are given below, one labelled as
Assertion (A) and the other labelled as
Reason (R):
Assertion (A): In a parliamentary form of government it is not the lower house which controls the executive but the executive which controls the house.
Reason (R): The Council of Ministers is constituted from within the legislature.
Choose the correct answer from among the codes given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
38.x: In the parliamentary form the executive is collectively responsible to and controlled by the lower house (Art. 75(3)), so A as a statement of the system is false; R is true – the Council of Ministers is drawn from the legislature.

38.s: What is a system with a few members and under the control of a group called?
38.x: Rule by a few members under the control of a group is oligarchy, which this option calls "minority system of governance". Gerontocracy is rule by the old, and anarchy is the absence of government.

38.s: Which of the following is a demerit of the presidential system?
o: Frequent fall of governments through no-confidence motions
38.x: Executive-legislature deadlock (and a personality cult around a single executive) are demerits of the presidential system; it has a fixed tenure.
xa: Avoiding **US-style executive-legislature conflict** was a reason the Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary form.
The risk of a **personality cult** under a single executive was another reason.
Parliamentary demerit: **cabinet dictatorship** when the majority is large.

38.s: 'Cabinet dictatorship' with a large majority is a demerit of which system?
38.x: Cabinet dictatorship under a large majority is listed as a demerit of the parliamentary system; deadlock and personality cult are presidential demerits.

38.s: Which of the following is a merit of the presidential system?
o: Fresh elections to break a deadlock
38.x: Stability of a fixed-term executive is the presidential merit; the other three are merits of the parliamentary system.

38.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, which two things can a democracy not maximise together?
38.x: Ambedkar said a democracy cannot maximise stability and responsibility together, so the parliamentary form does not guarantee both.

38.s: From working which Acts did the Constituent Assembly gain familiarity with parliamentary government?
38.x: Familiarity under the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935 was one reason for choosing the parliamentary form.

38.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, to what did India's choice of government give greater weight?
o: Responsibility and continuous accountability over guaranteed tenure
38.x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility. India chose responsibility, meaning continuous accountability, over guaranteed tenure.
38.tq: Distinguish the two competing values identified by Ambedkar and identify the one preferred by India.
xs: India chose **responsibility** — **continuous accountability** — **over guaranteed tenure** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar** held that a democracy cannot maximise **both stability and responsibility**.
Options (3) and (4) describe the **presidential** choice (fixed tenure, executive independence).
xa: **Vasant Sathe** made early proposals for a presidential system in the **1970s-80s**.
**NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02)** advised keeping the **parliamentary system**.
Parliamentary merit: the executive is **continuously accountable** to the legislature.

38.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Vasant Sathe — proposals for a presidential form in the 1970s–80s
Venkatachaliah Commission — recommendation to replace parliamentary government with a presidential system
One Nation, One Election — amendment only to Article 74
Dr B.R. Ambedkar — advocacy of guaranteed executive tenure over accountability
38.x: Vasant Sathe was associated with proposals for a presidential form of government in India during the 1970s–80s. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution advised retaining the parliamentary system, while the relevant One Nation, One Election proposal concerns Articles 83, 172 and 327.
38.tq: Use the person–proposal match and eliminate options that reverse the recommendation or alter the constitutional provisions.
xs: **Vasant Sathe** made early proposals for a **presidential system** in the **1970s-80s** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Venkatachaliah** Commission (NCRWC) advised **keeping** the parliamentary system, so (2) is wrong.
**One Nation, One Election** amends **Articles 83, 172 and 327**, not only Art. 74 — (3) is wrong.
**Ambedkar** favoured **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure — (4) is wrong.
xa: NCRWC worked during **2000-02**.
Critics: fixing tenures **grafts presidential mechanics** onto parliamentary democracy and **weakens accountability**.

38.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Shamsher Singh (1974)?
o: It is relevant to the limits parliamentary responsibility places on constitutional office-holders
It connected the Governor's conduct with the logic of the parliamentary system
It held public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor compatible with parliamentary conventions
38.x: Public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor was held to run counter to the parliamentary system.
xa: The President is the **de jure** head; real power lies with the **PM + Council of Ministers**.
⚠ The President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).

38.s: The One Nation, One Election proposal involves amendments to which Articles?
38.x: One Nation, One Election amends Articles 83, 172 and 327; critics say fixed tenures graft presidential mechanics onto the system.

38.s: Who proposed a presidential form of government for India in the 1970s-80s?
38.x: Vasant Sathe proposed a presidential form; the NCRWC under Venkatachaliah advised keeping the parliamentary system.

38.s: What did the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2000-02) advise about India's form of government?
o: Have a directly elected Prime Minister
38.x: The NCRWC headed by M.N. Venkatachaliah advised keeping the parliamentary system.

39.s: State Governor in India holds office during the pleasure of:
39.x: Art. 156(1): the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (in effect the Union Council of Ministers) – not Parliament, the Election Commission or the PM.

39.x: Both correct: the 7th Amendment (1956) allows one person to be Governor of two or more States, and in each State he acts on the advice of that State's own Council of Ministers.

o: Governor is not answerable to either House of the State
Governor is not answerable to either House of the Parliament
Governor is not answerable to Council of Ministers
Governor shall quit his office immediately after expiry of his term
39.x: Wrong statement: the Governor does not quit immediately when his five years end – he continues until his successor enters office (Art. 156(3)). He is not answerable to either House of the State, of Parliament, or to the Council of Ministers.

39.s: In relation to the Governor all following statements are correct, except
o: Governor is not answerable to either house of the state
Governor is not answerable to either house of the parliament
Governor not answerable to Council of Ministers
Governor has a fixed term of 5 years and he cannot be removed in between

39.x: Wrong statement: the five-year term is not fixed – the Governor holds office at the President's pleasure and can be removed at any time. The other three (not answerable to the State Houses, Parliament or the Council of Ministers) are correct.

39.s: Who is the executive head of the state?
39.x: The Governor is the executive head of the State (Art. 154); the CM heads the Council of Ministers (real executive).

39.s: Nominal executive head of a State in India

39.x: The Governor is the nominal (constitutional) executive head of the State; the CM and Council of Ministers are the real executive.

39.s: Regarding the Governor, all the following | C) statements are correct, EXCEPT-45.
o: The Governor is appointed by the President
The Governor acts as the constitutional head of the state
Governor shall quit his office immediately after expiry of his term
The Governor can reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President
39.x: Wrong statement: the Governor does not vacate office immediately when his term ends – he continues until his successor assumes office (Art. 156(3)). He is appointed by the President, is the constitutional head and can reserve Bills.

39.s: According to the constitution Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 which Article provides that there shall be a Governor for each State. 39.x: Art. 153 provides a Governor for each State; the 7th Amendment (1956) added the proviso allowing one person to be Governor of two or more States.

39.s: Which one of the following statements is correct?
o: In India, the same person cannot be appointed as Governor for two or more States at the same time
The Judges of the High Court of the States in India are appointed by the Governor of the State just as the
No procedure has been laid down in the Constitution of India for the removal of a Governor from his/her
In the case of a Union Territory having a legislative setup, the Chief Minister is appointed by the Lt.
39.x: Correct: the Constitution lays down no procedure or grounds for removing a Governor – he holds office at the President's pleasure. One person can govern two States (7th Amendment); HC judges are appointed by the President; a UT CM is appointed by the President.

39.s:

39.x: Art. 155: the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Art. 153 = a Governor for each State, 154 = executive power, 156 = term.

39.s:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :

39.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as

39.x: (A) is false: the 7th Amendment (1956) proviso to Art. 153 lets the same person be Governor of two or more States. (R) is true: Art. 153 says there shall be a Governor for each State.

39.x: Art. 155 is the appointment of the Governor (by the President by warrant), so the pair given for Art. 155 is wrong; Arts. 153, 154 and 156 (Governor for each State, executive power, term) were correctly matched.

39.s: What is the minimum age for becoming a Governor of State in India?
39.x: Art. 157 requires a Governor to be a citizen of India who has completed 35 years of age.

39.s: Who is the Constitutional Head of the State Government?
39.x: The Governor is the nominal or constitutional head of the State; the CM is the real head of the Government.

39.s: State Governor is appointed by
39.x: Under Art. 155 the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (on the Union Cabinet's advice, but the appointing authority is the President).

39.s: Which of the following qualifications for the office of the Governor is wrongly listed?
o: He or she must be a citizen of India
He or she must not be less than 30 years age
He or she must not be a member of either House of Parliament or a State Legislature
He or she must not hold any other office of profit
39.x: Wrongly listed: Art. 157 requires completion of 35 years, not 30. Citizenship, not being an MP/MLA and holding no office of profit are correct conditions (Arts. 157-158).

39.s: Which one of the following statements about the Governor of an Indian State is not true:
o: He is appointed by the President of India
He can be Governor of more than one State
He holds office for a term of five years
He can be removed earlier if the Legislature of the
39.x: Not true: the State Legislature has no power to remove the Governor – he holds office at the President's pleasure. He is appointed by the President, may govern two States and normally has a five-year term.

39.s: To whom is the Governor of a State responsible?
39.x: The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (Art. 156(1)) and is responsible to him – not to the PM, the Assembly or the CM.

39.s: Which of the following is correct?
o: Governor should not be a member of state legislature
Governor's normal term of office is 5 years
39.x: All are correct: the Governor cannot be a member of the State Legislature (Art. 158), is appointed by the President (Art. 155) and has a normal five-year term (Art. 156).

39.s: Under which Amendment to constitution, Governor can be appointed for one or more states?
39.x: The 7th Amendment, 1956 added the proviso to Art. 153 allowing one person to be Governor of two or more States.

39.s: Under Article 153 of the Constitution, which of the following is permissible?
o: A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States
A State may function without a Governor for an indefinite period
Only Union Territories can have a common Governor
A Governor may be elected jointly by two State Legislatures
39.x: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State, while the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 enables one person to serve as Governor of two or more States.
39.tq: Test the constitutional exception to the general rule instead of choosing the broad statement.
xs: **A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 153** provides a Governor for each state; the **7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956** lets **one person be Governor of 2 or more states**.
The Governor is **neither directly nor indirectly elected** — he is appointed by the **President** (Art. 155), so option (4) is wrong.
xa: With a **common Governor**, the cost is **shared among the states** as the President decides.
**E.S.L. Narasimhan** was the common Governor for **AP and Telangana**, **2014 to July 2019**.
The 7th Amendment point was asked in **APPSC-GS 2025** and **2021**.

39.s: Until when does a Governor continue in office after completing his normal term of five years?
o: The State Legislature passes a resolution
The next general election to the Assembly
39.x: The normal term is five years, but the Governor continues in office until the successor enters office.

39.s: Who determines the emoluments of a Governor?
39.x: Under Article 158, a Governor's emoluments are fixed by Parliament by law, not by the State Legislature.

41.s: Which of the following statement(s) is/are NOT one of the powers of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly?

He has no veto except in case of a tie
The Speaker will NOT preside when a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration of the Assembly

Most keys (APPSC Group-1 2022): Both (B) and (C). Strictly: (A) is also 'not a power' – the Speaker has only a casting vote (Art. 189), voting in the first instance only on a resolution for his own removal (Art. 181).
B (a vote only in a tie) and C (does not preside over his own removal resolution) are limits, not powers – hence the official key 'Both B and C'. A is also untrue: the Speaker has no original vote in all matters.

41.s: If the Speaker of Legislative Assembly of a State wants to resign, he will give his resignation to –

xs: The State Legislature is in **Part VI, Articles 168–212** — so option **(1)** is correct.

Being of unsound mind as declared by a competent court

o: Supremacy of the Constitution and limited government
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
44.x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government. India combines elements of American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary supremacy, while Parliament remains subject to the Constitution.
44.tq: Reject absolute formulations and identify the constitutional limitation underlying review.
xs: The theory behind judicial review is **supremacy of the Constitution and limited government** — option **(3)** is correct.
Not unlimited judicial supremacy, absolute parliamentary sovereignty, or executive supremacy.
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: ⚠ Judicial review = symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key); theory = **supremacy of the Constitution**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + FRs.
SC (**17 May 2026**): **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

44.s: Judicial review in India is regarded as a symbol of which of the following?
44.x: Judicial review is a symbol of federal government: courts act as umpire of the Centre-State division under a written, supreme Constitution. Parliamentary, unitary and presidential forms do not by themselves require such an umpire.
44.tq: Judicial review = symbol of federalism; theory = supremacy of the Constitution.
xs: Judicial review is a symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key) — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire of the Centre-State division** under a **written, supreme Constitution**.
Parliamentary, unitary or presidential forms do not by themselves need such an umpire.
xa: Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.
**Art. 131**: SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State** disputes.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
44.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
44.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
xs: **Disagreement with the majority party's policy** is NOT a ground of review — option **(2)** is the answer.
The three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of constitutional provisions / Basic Structure**.
xa: Courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
**State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977)**: SC declined a political question → **restraint**.
Writs are **discretionary** — refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.

44.s: Under which US Chief Justice was Marbury v. Madison (1803), the origin of judicial review, decided?
44.x: Marbury v. Madison (1803) was decided under Chief Justice John Marshall; its roots go back to Sir Edward Coke.

44.s: In which case was it first held that Fundamental Rights can be amended by Parliament?
44.x: Shankari Prasad (1951) first held that Fundamental Rights are amendable.

44.s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
44.x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
44.tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
xs: Decisions can be reviewed for **mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example: President's Rule reviewed in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
Popularity or mere policy disagreement are not grounds.
xa: **Art. 361**: the **President/Governor** personally are **not answerable** to courts.
**Art. 74(2)** / **163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into**.
**44th Amendment (1978)** reversed the **38th**'s non-justiciability bar.

44.s: Which Article bars courts from inquiring into the advice of Ministers to the President?
44.x: Article 74(2) is the bar for advice to the President; Article 163(3) for advice to the Governor.
xa: **No mandamus** lies against the President/Governor (TH, **29 Jan 2026**).
Their decisions may still be reviewed for **mala fides** — **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

44.s: Which Article makes legislative power subject to the provisions of the Constitution?
44.x: Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution; Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy.
xa: **Lack of legislative competence** is one of the **three grounds** of review.
**Art. 13**: laws inconsistent with FRs are **void**.

44.s: Under which Article do the High Courts share judicial review with the Supreme Court through their writ jurisdiction?
44.x: The Supreme Court holds writ power under Article 32 and the High Courts under Article 226, so judicial review is shared.
n: The Supreme Court exercises Judicial Review under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
The High Courts exercise Judicial Review under Article 226. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is vested jointly in the Supreme Court and the High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 32 provides the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 226 provides the High Courts' writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]

44.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court

**Arts. 251, 254**: **repugnancy**.

44.s: Which Article is the primary textual foundation for striking down laws that abridge Fundamental Rights?
44.x: Article 13(2) makes laws abridging Fundamental Rights void; review of the Court's own judgments is Article 137 and complete justice is Article 142.
n: Article 13(2) is an express constitutional basis for striking down ultra vires laws. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 137 gives the Supreme Court the power to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 137 provides for review of the Supreme Court's own judgment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass decrees or orders for Complete Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]

44.x: Article 163(3) bars inquiry into advice to the Governor; Article 74(2) does so for the President.

Amendments overcoming judgments remain subject to the **basic structure**.

44.s: Who was the Chief Justice of India when public interest litigation (PIL) was introduced to the Indian Judicial System?

Most books and keys (UPSC 2006): P.N. Bhagwati, the judge who introduced PIL. Strictly: when the first PILs were admitted (1979-81) the CJI was Y.V. Chandrachud (1978-85); Bhagwati was CJI only in 1985-86 (sci.gov.in former CJIs list).
P.N. Bhagwati (with V.R. Krishna Iyer) introduced PIL and later became CJI (1985-86), which is why UPSC keyed him. Hidayatullah (1968-70), Ahmadi (1994-97) and Anand (1998-2001) had nothing to do with PIL's start.

44.x: PIL is the most popular form and outcome of judicial activism, which began in India in the mid-1970s. Judicial review is the basis of activism, not the thing activism is 'related to' in this standard question.

44.s: Who was the Chief Justice of India when Public Interest litigation was introduced in the Indian Judicial System?
44.x:
Most books and keys (UPPCS 2018, UPSC 2006): P.N. Bhagwati, the judge who introduced PIL. Strictly: when the first PILs were admitted (1979-81) the CJI was Y.V. Chandrachud (1978-85); Bhagwati was CJI only in 1985-86 (sci.gov.in former CJIs list).
P.N. Bhagwati (with V.R. Krishna Iyer) introduced PIL and later became CJI (1985-86), so he is the keyed answer. Hidayatullah, Ahmadi and Anand were CJIs at other times and are unconnected with PIL's origin.

xa: **Precedence:** **Union List > Concurrent List > State List**.
**Article 246A** (**101st Amendment, 2016**) gives **simultaneous** GST power to Parliament and States.

47.s: Under Article 246(4), on matters in which Lists may Parliament legislate for areas not included in a State (Union Territories)?
o: The Union and Concurrent Lists only
47.x: Article 246(4) lets Parliament legislate for areas not included in a State on matters in all three Lists, not merely the Union List.
xa: **President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.

47.s: Which Article empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on GST?
47.x: Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016, gives Parliament and State Legislatures simultaneous power to make GST laws; only Parliament makes laws on inter-State supply.
n: Article 246A gives Parliament simultaneous power to frame laws regarding Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 246A gives State Legislatures simultaneous power to frame laws regarding Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 246A breaks the strict exclusive-list dichotomy of Article 246. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Panchayati Raj is enumerated in the State List under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Municipalities are enumerated in the State List under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

47.s: The Union List and Concurrent List originally had 97 and 47 subjects. How many do they have today?
47.x: The Union List now has 98 subjects (97 originally) and the Concurrent List 52 (47 originally).
xa: Some notes (UPSC) give the present counts as **100 / 61 / 52**.
⚠ **Safe exam fact:** original **97/66/47**.
**Entry 97** of the Union List is also the **residuary** entry.

47.s: Which Constitutional Amendment omitted Entries 52 and 55 of the State List?
47.x: The 101st Amendment (GST) omitted State Entries 52 and 55; the 42nd omitted 11, 19, 20, 29 and the 7th omitted 36.

47.s: Over which List does Article 246(3) give State Legislatures exclusive power?
47.x: Under Article 246(3) States have exclusive power over List II, subject to clauses (1) and (2).

47.s: Under Article 246A, who alone can make GST laws on inter-State supply of goods and services?
47.x: Article 246A gives Parliament and States simultaneous GST power, but only Parliament legislates on inter-State supply (IGST).

47.s: Which Constitutional Amendment omitted Entry 36 of the State List?
47.x: Entry 36 went with the 7th Amendment (1956); entries 11, 19, 20 and 29 with the 42nd, and 52 and 55 with the 101st.

47.s: In which List does preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State and public order fall?
47.x: Concurrent List Entry 3 covers preventive detention for State security and public order, while Union List Entry 9 covers it for defence, foreign affairs and security of India.
xa: The **Allahabad HC** criticised the **routine use** of preventive detention.

47.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List
47.x: Agriculture is a State List subject, so B is correct. Trade and commerce within a State is a State List subject (not Union), while currency and foreign loans are Union List subjects (not State or Concurrent).
47.tq: Use the list allocation of familiar subjects to eliminate swapped entries.
xs: **Agriculture — State List** — option **(2)**.
Trade and commerce **within** a State is a **State** subject, not Union (option 1).
**Currency** and **foreign loans** are **Union** subjects (options 3 and 4 wrong).
xa: ⚠ **Inter-state** trade = Union; trade **within** a State = State.
Farm Laws used Concurrent **Entry 33** although agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
Other State subjects: **public health and sanitation**, **markets**, **fisheries**.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about preservation of livestock (cow slaughter)?
o: Parliament can legislate on it through Articles 249, 250 or 252
Preservation of livestock is a State List subject
Article 48 is relevant to constitutional policy on preservation of livestock
Parliament may legislate on it only through the ordinary Union List power
47.x: Being a State subject, Parliament can legislate on it through routes such as Articles 249, 250 or 252, not through the ordinary Union List power.
xa: **Prevention of cruelty to animals** is a separate **Concurrent** subject (**Entry 17**).
Parliament can reach State subjects only via **Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253, 356**.

47.s: Which of the following examples has been cited in debates concerning use of the Concurrent List to reach State subjects?
o: Farm Laws through Concurrent List Entry 33
Currency regulation through State List Entry 15
Foreign affairs through Concurrent List Entry 3
47.x: Farm Laws were discussed as an example of Concurrent List Entry 33 being used in a field associated with agriculture, which is State List Entry 14.
47.tq: Match the debated law with the relevant Concurrent List entry and the associated State subject.
xs: **Farm Laws** were made via **Concurrent List Entry 33** — option **(2)**.
Critics say this reached a **State** subject, as agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
**Census**, **currency** and **foreign affairs** are **Union** subjects, so the other options are wrong.
xa: The **NEP** and **NMC Act** are also cited in the Concurrent List encroachment debate.
Other centralising tools: **Art. 254(2)** override; **Art. 249/252** use.
**Frequent ordinances** and **Union List dominance** are also criticised.

47.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out with reference to the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule?
47.x: Fisheries is a State List subject. Succession, criminal law and civil procedure are subjects in the Concurrent List.
47.tq: Identify the subject belonging to a different list rather than relying on a familiar association.
xs: **Fisheries** is a **State** subject — the odd one out — option **(3)**.
**Criminal law**, **succession** and **civil procedure** are all **Concurrent** subjects.
xa: Other State subjects: **public health and sanitation**, **agriculture**, **markets**.
Other Concurrent subjects: **adulteration** of foodstuffs, marriage and divorce, **drugs**, **electricity**, **newspapers**.
Union subjects: **RBI**, **foreign loans**, banking, **currency**, **census**, **inter-state trade**.

Space research – Residuary subject under Article 248
47.x: Education is a Concurrent List subject, not Union List. Defence is Union, public order is State (Entry 1), and space research is residuary under Article 248.
n: Defence is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Armed forces are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Public order is a State List subject under Entry 1. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Education is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Corporation tax is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Public order belongs to the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Corporation tax belongs to the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Residuary basis: **Art. 248** + **Entry 97** of the Union List; covers residuary **taxation** too.
Other residuary example: **cyber law**.
Residuary powers lie with the **States** in the **USA** and **Australia**, with the **Centre** in **Canada** and **India**.

47.s: The constitutional basis for Parliament enacting the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act is primarily found in which entry?
47.x: Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in Concurrent List Entry 17, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.
47.tq: Distinguish the Concurrent List entry on animal cruelty from the State entry on preservation of livestock.
xs: **Prevention of cruelty to animals** is **Concurrent List Entry 17** — the basis of the central **Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act** — option **(1)**.
**State Entry 15** is **preservation of livestock**; **Concurrent Entry 33** was used for the **Farm Laws**.
xa: Cow slaughter: preservation of livestock = **State** subject (**Entry 15**) + DPSP **Art. 48**.
Other Concurrent subjects: **criminal law**, **civil procedure**, **succession**, **marriage and divorce**.

47.x: Adulteration of foodstuffs, drugs and electricity are Concurrent List subjects.

47.x: The 42nd Amendment moved forests and education, among others, from the State List to the Concurrent List.

47.x: Panchayats are a State subject (Entry 5), and Article 243-C(1) lets the State Legislature decide their composition.

47.x: This is Union List Entry 9; preventive detention for State security and public order is Concurrent Entry 3.

47.s:
The distribution of legislative power is well-defined in most cases under the Indian Constitution. In this context, which of body have legislative power to make extraterritorial legislation in India?

1. Parliament only

2. Lok Sabha only

3. Rajya Sabha only

4. President with the advice of the Prime Minister

5. State Legislature

6. Indian Government with the approval of the United Nations
47.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
47.x: Art. 245(2): no law of Parliament is invalid for extra-territorial operation, so only Parliament can make extra-territorial laws; a State law reaches outside only with a territorial nexus. Neither House alone, the President, the State Legislature nor any 'UN approval' has this power.

47.s: With respect to the Indian federalism, which of the following statements about the 'Doctrine of Territorial Nexus' is correct?
o: The Doctrine of Territorial Nexus has been used in the cases to decide questions of competency to enact a law.
The Doctrine of Territorial Nexus is based on the concept of equity and fairness in legal proceedings.
The doctrine implies that what cannot be done directly should not be done indirectly.
It determines the scope of state legislatures' extra-territorial power to enact laws.
47.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
47.x: The doctrine of territorial nexus decides when a State law with extra-territorial operation is valid: there must be a sufficient, real nexus between the State and the object. 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' is colourable legislation.

47.s:
The Parliament of India has the 'Power to Legislate' for the following–
1. Union of India
2. Territory of India
3. Indian subject resident and their property situated anywhere in the world
Select the correct answer from the code given below– Code–
47.x: Parliament legislates for the whole or any part of the territory of India and, since its laws may operate extra-territorially (Art. 245(2)), for Indian citizens and their property anywhere in the world – so all three.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the territorial extent of laws?
o: Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India
A parliamentary law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation
A State Legislature may ordinarily legislate for another State's territory without any territorial connection
A State law needs a sufficient territorial nexus for extra-territorial reach
47.x: A State law requires a sufficient territorial nexus for any extra-territorial reach, so the last statement is false.
xa: ⚠ **Extra-territorial** laws = Parliament only; State needs **territorial nexus**.
**President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.
The **Governor** can bar or modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.

47.s: Who makes regulations having the force of Acts of Parliament for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep?
o: Chief Secretary of the Union Territory
47.x: Regulations made by the President for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
xa: The **Governor** can bar/modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.
The **Governor of Assam** has a similar role for Assam tribal areas.

47.s: In Scheduled Areas, who may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament?
47.x: The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas.
xa: The **Governor of Assam** has a similar power for **Assam tribal areas**.
**President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** carry the force of Parliament's Acts.
⚠ **Extra-territorial** laws = Parliament only.

47.s: Who can make laws with extra-territorial operation?
47.x: Only Parliament can make extra-territorial laws (Article 245(2)); a State law needs a territorial nexus.

47.s: When may a State law reach outside the State?
47.x: A State legislature makes laws for its own State; outside reach is valid only with a real territorial nexus.

47.s: The doctrine of " Paramountcy " is a legal principle:
o: to reconcile conflicting laws where both central government and Provincial governments have the power to create laws in relation to the same matter
To explain the law making authority of the Government
To provide law making authority to the Central government
To explain law making authority of the country
47.x: The doctrine of paramountcy reconciles conflicting laws where both the Centre and the States can legislate on the same matter: the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy (Art. 254).

47.s: Articles 301 to 303 principally restrict Parliament from doing which of the following in relation to trade and commerce?
o: Making any law concerning inter-State trade
47.x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.
47.tq: Distinguish a restriction against discrimination from a complete prohibition on regulation.
xs: **Arts. 301-303** stop Parliament from **preferring or discriminating between States** in trade laws — option **(1)**.
Discrimination is allowed only in **scarcity**.
xa: State restrictions on **inter-state trade**: reasonable, in **public interest**, with **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, **Arts. 301-305**).
**Inter-state trade** is a **Union** subject; trade **within** a State is a State subject.

47.s: Whose previous sanction does a State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest require?
47.x: A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but such a Bill needs the President's previous sanction.
xa: **Art. 255**: recommendations and previous sanctions are **matters of procedure only** — later **assent** cures the defect.
**Inter-state** trade = **Union**; trade **within** a State = **State**.

47.s: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025 was reported in connection with which issue?
o: Deemed assent and timelines for Governors and the President
Allocation of residuary powers to States
Transfer of forests to the Union List
47.x: The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.
47.tq: Identify the constitutional controversy from the paired concepts rather than from a general federalism label.
xs: The SC advisory opinion (**Nov 2025**) rejected **deemed assent** and **fixed timelines** for **Governors/President** — option **(1)**.
It concerns assent to State bills, linked to **Art. 254(2)** reservation by the Governor.
xa: Under **254(2)**, the Governor may reserve a bill as an exception to **aid-and-advice**.
A State law with **President's assent** prevails **in that State**.
Parliament can later **override** it with a fresh law.

47.s: Under Article 251, which law prevails if a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 conflicts with a State law?
o: both laws become void to the extent of conflict
47.x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.
xa: The **State legislature's power is not suspended** under Art. 249 or 250.
**Art. 249** law ceases **6 months after the resolution lapses**; **Art. 250** law **6 months** after the emergency.

47.s: Which of the following is INCORRECT about repugnancy on Concurrent List subjects?
o: Repugnancy is dealt with under Article 250.
In a conflict, the Central law generally prevails.
The Central-law rule has an exception relating to Presidential assent.
A reserved State law that gets Presidential assent may prevail under Article 254(2).
47.x: Repugnancy on Concurrent subjects is dealt with by Article 254, not Article 250 (Emergency legislation).
n: Article 254 governs repugnancy between Central and State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Central legislation prevails when it conflicts with State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

A State law can prevail over conflicting Central legislation when the State law was reserved for the President’s assent and received that assent under Article 254(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: **Proviso:** Parliament can later **override** such a State law with a **fresh law**.
**Article 250** = Parliament on the State List during an **Emergency**.

47.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 254(2)?
o: A repugnant State law on a Concurrent List subject prevails in that State if it receives the President's assent
The State law must be reserved for the consideration of the President
Parliament can later amend or repeal such a State law by a fresh law
Such a State law, once assented to, prevails throughout India
47.x: A State law assented to under Article 254(2) prevails only in that State, not throughout India.
xa: Repugnancy applies to the **Concurrent List** field.

47.s: 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' is the principle behind which doctrine?
47.x: This maxim underlies the doctrine of colourable legislation, which checks whether a legislature crosses its competence under a permissible guise.
n: The principle of Colorable Legislation is that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Colorable Legislation concerns transgression of legislative competence masked under a permissible guise. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Case: **Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952)**; basis **Article 246**.
⚠ Other notes cite **K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953)**.
⚠ **Balsara (1951)** = pith and substance; **Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)** = colourable legislation.

47.s: Which case upheld a State prohibition law under the doctrine of pith and substance?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa
47.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition law was upheld under pith and substance; its incidental encroachment did not change its true character.
xa: ⚠ **Balsara (1951)** = pith and substance; **Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)** = colourable legislation.
**Harmonious construction**: entries read together so both operate.
**Repugnancy (Art. 254)**: Union law prevails in the **Concurrent** field.

47.s: Which doctrine requires legislative entries to be read together so that each can operate harmoniously?
47.x: Harmonious construction requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.
47.tq: Discriminate among neighbouring doctrines by their operative principle.
xs: **Harmonious construction** reads entries together so that **both operate** — option **(2)**.
**Pith and substance** looks at a law's **true nature**; **repugnancy** (**Art. 254**) makes Union law prevail; **colourable legislation** bars doing indirectly what cannot be done directly.
xa: Pith and substance case: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)**.
Colourable legislation case: **K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953)**.
Under **254(2)**, a State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.

47.s: What is the effect of the Doctrine of Severability?
o: The whole statute is declared void
Only the unconstitutional part is declared void, if separable
A law is tested only by its title
Parliament must re-enact the entire law
47.x: Under severability, only the unconstitutional part of a law is struck down if it can be separated; the rest survives.
n: Only the offending or unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void under the Doctrine of Severability. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The valid portion of a statute remains intact under the Doctrine of Severability if it can be separated from the offending portion. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Cases: **A.K. Gopalan (1950)** and **State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)**.
⚠ **Eclipse** concerns **pre-constitutional** laws, which stay **dormant**, not permanently void.
Most doctrines are **judicially evolved**, not written in the Constitution.

47.s: Which doctrine holds that a pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a Fundamental Right stays dormant and revives if that right is amended?
47.x: Under the doctrine of eclipse such a law is not dead ab initio but only overshadowed, and it revives when the right is amended.
n: Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio under the Doctrine of Eclipse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights remain overshadowed or dormant under the Doctrine of Eclipse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
A pre-constitutional law eclipsed by Fundamental Rights becomes active if the relevant Fundamental Right is amended. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: **Severability:** only the **offending portion** is void.
**Basic Structure:** **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Article 368**.

47.s: What does judicial review by the higher judiciary test the constitutional validity of?
o: Both legislative acts and executive actions
47.x: Judicial review is the higher judiciary's power to test both laws and executive action.
n: Most constitutional doctrines in India are not expressly defined in the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Most constitutional doctrines in India are not written in the text of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]

The higher judiciary, comprising the Supreme Court and High Courts, can adjudicate the constitutional validity of legislative acts and executive actions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Origin: **Marbury v. Madison (1803)** — **John Marshall** (USA).
**Colorable legislation:** **Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952)**.

47.s: Which doctrine looks at the true nature of a law and ignores its incidental encroachment on another List?
47.x: The doctrine of pith and substance resolves overlaps between the Lists by examining the law's true nature.
n: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance resolves overlaps between legislative fields. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Pith and Substance examines the true nature and essence of a law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Incidental encroachment by a law on another legislative List does not determine its validity under the Doctrine of Pith and Substance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]

47.s: The Doctrine of Eclipse is associated with which case?
o: Prafulla Kumar v Bank of Commerce
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of M.P.
Kameshwar Singh v State of Bihar
A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras
47.x: The Doctrine of Eclipse comes from Bhikaji Narain Dhakras; Prafulla Kumar is a pith and substance case.
n: The Doctrine of Severability originated in A.K. Gopalan (1950) and State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Eclipse originated in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Pith and Substance originated in Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce (1947) and State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The Doctrine of Colorable Legislation originated in Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]

47.s: With which doctrine is K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953) linked?
47.x: Gajapati Narayan Deo and Kameshwar Singh are colourable legislation cases: what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

47.s: In which case did the Privy Council apply the doctrine of pith and substance in 1947?
o: State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara
Kameshwar Singh v State of Bihar
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v State of M.P.
47.x: Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce (1947) is the Privy Council case on pith and substance.

47.s: With which case is the origin of judicial review associated?
47.x: Judicial review traces to Marbury v Madison (1803) in the USA.
